How Machine Learning Models Are Trained: From Raw Data to Deployed AI
A technical guide to how machine learning models are trained—covering learning paradigms, data pipelines, loss functions, optimization, distributed hardware, and post-training.

blocks.text: From Code to Weights: What Training Actually Means

blocks.html: Conventional software is written by hand. A programmer anticipates the conditions a system will face, encodes explicit rules, and compiles those instructions into deterministic logic. Machine learning flips that workflow on its head. Instead of writing rules to map inputs to outputs, engineers define a flexible mathematical structure—a model—and expose it to vast quantities of data so the system discovers the mapping itself.

At initialization, a neural network knows nothing. Its internal parameters, called weights and biases, are filled with small random numbers. Fed a medical radiograph, an audio waveform, or the opening sentence of a legal brief, an untrained model outputs numerical noise. Training is the iterative computational process that nudges those millions or hundreds of billions of parameters until the model's outputs consistently match a desired target or structure.

What makes modern training remarkable is not a single breakthrough, but a tightly coupled stack of disciplines: statistical learning theory, large-scale data engineering, numerical optimization, high-performance systems architecture, and human-guided behavioral alignment. A single training run for a frontier model now coordinates tens of thousands of specialized silicon processors over months, consumes megawatts of electricity, and executes upward of 1025 floating-point operations (FLOPs) [26]. Yet the underlying mathematical
heartbeat—measuring error and adjusting weights to reduce it—remains recognizable from experiments conducted nearly seven decades ago.

blocks.text: A Brief History of Machine Learning Training

blocks.html: The lineage of modern training begins in 1958, when psychologist Frank Rosenblatt introduced the Perceptron at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory [1]. Rosenblatt modeled a single

artificial neuron that computed a weighted sum of binary inputs and applied a threshold to classify patterns. When the Perceptron made a mistake, a simple update rule nudged its weights in the direction of the correct answer. It proved that a machine could adjust its own internal state from examples, though single-layer Perceptrons could only solve linearly separable problems—meaning they failed on basic logic functions like exclusive-OR (XOR).

Unlocking multi-layer networks required a reliable way to assign credit—or blame—to intermediate "hidden" layers that never directly touch the final output. In October 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published a four-page paper in Nature demonstrating backpropagation: an application of the multivariable chain rule that propagates output errors backward through a network so every internal weight can be updated systematically [2]. Backpropagation enabled hidden layers to learn internal representations—
edges, shapes, syntactic roles—without human engineers designing those features by hand.

For two decades, deep networks still struggled against limited datasets, vanishing gradients, and modest central processing unit (CPU) speeds. That ceiling shattered in 2012. Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton trained a deep convolutional neural network— later known as AlexNet—on more than 1.2 million labeled images across 1,000 categories for the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge [3]. Running across two consumer

NVIDIA GTX 580 graphics processing units (GPUs) with 3 GB of memory each, AlexNet achieved a top-5 test error rate of 15.3%, beating the second-place entry's 26.2% by more than ten percentage points [3]. The result established a template that still governs the field: pair deep architectures with large datasets and parallel GPU acceleration.
The next structural inflection arrived in June 2017, when Ashish Vaswani and seven colleagues at Google published Attention Is All You Need, introducing the Transformer architecture [7].

Previous sequence models—recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks—processed tokens one step at a time, creating a sequential bottleneck that restricted hardware parallelization. By replacing recurrence entirely with self-attention mechanisms, the Transformer allowed an entire sequence to be processed simultaneously. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation benchmark, the model reached a state-of-the-art 41.8 BLEU score after just 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs [7]. Once training could
parallelize cleanly across sequences and across chips, the era of web-scale foundation models began.

Every training pipeline starts with a strategic choice: where does the learning signal come from? Machine learning organizes that choice into four primary paradigms, each suited to different data availability and task structures.

In supervised learning, every training example is paired with an explicit ground-truth label—an image labeled "melanoma," a credit transaction labeled "fraudulent," or a house listing paired with its closing price. The model predicts an output from the input, compares its prediction against the label, and adjusts its parameters to shrink the discrepancy. Supervised learning powers high-precision diagnostic classifiers, demand forecasting, and structured tabular modeling. Its primary constraint is economic and logistical: human annotation is slow, expensive, and difficult to scale to billions of examples.

Unsupervised learning removes labels altogether. Given raw, unannotated inputs, the algorithm searches for latent structure—grouping similar customers through clustering (such as k-means or hierarchical clustering), compressing high-dimensional measurements into lower-dimensional manifolds via principal component analysis (PCA) or autoencoders, or flagging anomalous sensor readings that deviate from normal operating distributions. Because no target label exists, evaluation is less straightforward, often relying on reconstruction error, cluster cohesion, or downstream utility.

Self-supervised learning bridges the gap by manufacturing supervisory signals directly from unlabeled data. Rather than asking humans to annotate text or images, the training objective hides part of an input and forces the model to predict the missing piece from context.

In natural language processing, two self-supervised formulations reshaped the field. In October 2018, Google researchers introduced BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), which randomly masks words inside a sentence and trains the network to reconstruct them using both left and right context [11]. Autoregressive language models—the

family behind modern generative assistants—use an even simpler objective: next-token prediction, where every token in a document serves as the target label for all tokens preceding it. In computer vision, contrastive self-supervised frameworks such as SimCLR (published by Ting Chen, Simon Kornblith, Mohammad Norouzi, and Geoffrey Hinton in 2020) create two differently augmented views of the same image—via random cropping and color distortion—and train the network to pull those paired views together in embedding space while pushing views of different images apart [17]. On ImageNet, a linear classifier placed atop
SimCLR's self-supervised representations reached 76.5% top-1 accuracy, matching a fully supervised ResNet-50, and fine-tuning on just 1% of labels achieved 85.8% top-5 accuracy [17].

Reinforcement learning (RL) operates in an interactive loop rather than on a static dataset. An agent observes the state of an environment, selects an action according to its policy, and receives a scalar reward signal. The objective is to learn a policy that maximizes cumulative expected reward over time. Because rewards are often delayed—a chess move may only pay off twenty turns later—RL must solve the temporal credit-assignment problem while balancing exploration of untried actions against exploitation of known high-reward strategies.
Modern deep RL relies heavily on policy-gradient methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), introduced by John Schulman and colleagues in July 2017 [8]. PPO

optimizes a clipped surrogate objective that prevents any single gradient update from shifting the policy too far from its previous behavior, delivering stable convergence across simulated robotics, game playing, and—more recently—large language model alignment [8] [19].

blocks.html: Experienced machine learning engineers treat data pipelines with the same rigor as model architecture. No optimization algorithm can rescue a corrupted, duplicated, or leaky dataset. In fact, as model architectures have converged around variants of the Transformer and gradient-boosted decision trees, data curation has become one of the sharpest differentiators of final model quality.

For tabular enterprise systems, curation means reconciling schema mismatches, imputing missing values without introducing bias, normalizing skewed numerical distributions, and auditing for class imbalance. For web-scale foundation models, the challenge is industrial text and media hygiene. Raw web crawls are flooded with boilerplate navigation menus, machine-translated spam, duplicated templates, and personally identifiable information (PII).

Modern pre-training pipelines—such as the one documented in Meta's Llama 3 Herd of Models technical report—pass raw web text through multi-stage filtering: heuristic rules strip malformed HTML and repetitive boilerplate, exact and near-duplicate deduplication (often using locality-sensitive hashing like MinHash) removes repeated documents that would otherwise cause memorization, and lightweight model-based classifiers score educational and linguistic quality before mixing domains such as web prose, source code, mathematics, and multilingual text [26].
Models operate on numbers, never directly on raw words, pixels, or timestamps. Converting raw observations into numerical tensors takes two distinct forms depending on the domain.

In classical machine learning and structured tabular domains—credit risk, fraud detection, supply-chain telemetry—feature engineering remains decisive. Practitioners construct domain-specific numerical representations: rolling 30-day transaction velocity, one-hot or target encodings for categorical variables, and interaction terms that expose non-linear relationships to linear models or decision trees.

In modern natural language processing, manual linguistic features have been replaced by subword tokenization. Character-level sequences are too long for efficient attention, while word-level vocabularies explode in size and fail on rare words, compound nouns, or morphological inflections. In 2015, Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch adapted Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)—originally a 1994 data compression algorithm—to neural machine translation [6]. BPE starts with individual characters or bytes and iteratively merges the most

frequent adjacent pairs until a target vocabulary size is reached (commonly 32,000 to over 128,000 tokens in contemporary LLMs). Common words remain single tokens, while rare words decompose cleanly into recognizable subword pieces—improving WMT 2015 English-German and English-Russian translation by 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU over dictionary back-off baselines [6].
Each token ID is then mapped to a dense, learnable vector called an embedding, which serves as the numerical entry point to the neural network.
To know whether a model has learned generalizable patterns rather than memorizing its training examples, practitioners partition data into three strictly isolated subsets:
1. Training set (commonly 70%–80% in classical datasets, or the vast majority of tokens in web-scale pre-training): used to compute gradients and update weights.

2. Validation set (often 10%–15%): never used to update weights directly, but evaluated periodically to tune hyperparameters (learning rate, regularization strength, architecture depth) and trigger early stopping.
3. Test set (held out until final evaluation): provides an unbiased estimate of real-world generalization.

When working with limited datasets, engineers frequently use k-fold cross-validation, rotating the validation fold across k partitions to reduce variance in performance estimates. Critically, splits must respect data structure: time-series forecasting requires chronological splits so future data never leaks into past training windows, and medical imaging requires patient-level splits so scans from the same person never appear in both training and test sets. Data leakage —whether through subtle preprocessing errors like computing normalization statistics across the entire dataset before splitting, or through web-scale benchmark contamination where public evaluation questions accidentally enter a pre-training crawl [26]—silently inflates
reported accuracy while leaving production reliability degraded. (For a deeper look at how models balance memorization and generalization, see Overfitting and Underfitting in Machine Learning.)

blocks.text: Objective Functions: Translating Goals into Mathematics

blocks.html: A machine learning model cannot "want" to diagnose a tumor or translate Japanese accurately; it can only minimize a differentiable scalar number called the loss function (or objective function), denoted ℒ(θ), where θ represents all trainable parameters. Choosing the right loss function is how engineers translate a real-world goal into a smooth geometric landscape that gradient-based optimizers can descend.
For continuous regression tasks—predicting kilowatt-hour grid load, asset volatility, or temperature—the standard objective is Mean Squared Error:

Squaring the residual ensures all errors are non-negative and penalizes large outliers disproportionately, yielding a smooth, convex surface for linear models. When datasets contain heavy outlier noise, practitioners often substitute Mean Absolute Error (MAE) or Huber loss to temper extreme gradients.

For classification and autoregressive language modeling, the model outputs a probability distribution over C discrete classes or vocabulary tokens (typically via the softmax function). The workhorse objective is Cross-Entropy Loss, which measures the divergence between the true distribution y and the predicted probability distribution p̂ :

assigning a 0.01 probability to the true class incurs a much steeper penalty than assigning 0.40, driving the network toward calibrated probability estimates.

In self-supervised representation learning and multimodal alignment (such as pairing images with captions), there is no fixed list of class labels. Instead, contrastive objectives—such as InfoNCE or the normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss (NT-Xent) used in SimCLR [17]—operate on similarities between vector embeddings. Given a positive pair of augmented views (i, j) with normalized embeddings zi and zj, cosine similarity sim(u, v) = u^T v / (‖u‖‖v‖), and
a temperature scaling parameter τ, the loss for pair (i, j) among 2N augmented samples in a batch is:

blocks.html: Minimizing this objective pushes matching representations closer on the hypersphere while repelling non-matching negatives. Because the denominator sums over all other examples in the batch, contrastive training benefits substantially from large batch sizes that supply rich negative comparisons [17].
With data prepared and an objective function defined, training enters its core iterative engine. Each step of the optimization loop follows four operations:

1. Forward pass: A mini-batch of inputs flows layer by layer through the model to produce predictions and evaluate the scalar loss ℒ(θ). Intermediate layer outputs (called activations) are cached in memory because they are needed to compute derivatives.

2. Backward pass (backpropagation): Using reverse-mode automatic differentiation, the system applies the chain rule from the output loss backward to the input layer, computing the gradient ∇θ ℒ—a vector indicating the direction and steepness of loss increase with respect to every single weight [2].
3. Parameter update: An optimizer uses those gradients to step the parameters downward toward lower loss.
4. Zeroing and repeating: Gradients are cleared (or accumulated across micro-batches) and the next batch enters the pipeline.
(For a step-by-step derivation of the chain rule and gradient geometry, see Gradient Descent and Backpropagation Explained.)

Computing the exact gradient over an entire dataset of millions of images or trillions of tokens before making a single weight update—known as full-batch gradient descent—is computationally prohibitive. Conversely, updating weights after every single example produces noisy, erratic trajectories and wastes the parallel matrix engines of modern accelerators.

Practitioners therefore use mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD), averaging gradients over a batch of B examples (or tokens) per step (iteration). One complete pass over the entire training dataset constitutes an epoch. Classic vision models might train for 90 to 300 epochs over ImageNet, whereas frontier language models trained on 15 trillion tokens often execute just one to a few epochs—or even a single pass over unique web text—because repeating data too many times degrades generalization [20] [26]. When desired global batch

sizes exceed available accelerator memory (often reaching several million tokens per step in large language models), engineers use gradient accumulation: running multiple smaller micro-batches sequentially, summing their gradients, and applying a single optimizer update.

In December 2014, Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba introduced Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation), which tracks both a running mean of gradients (first moment, mt) and a running uncentered variance of squared gradients (second moment, vt) for every individual parameter [5]:

Adam became the default optimizer for deep learning because it handles

However, in 2017, Ilya Loshchilov and Frank Hutter demonstrated a subtle flaw: adding standard L<sub>2</sub> weight penalties directly to the loss function inside Adam couples weight
shrinkage with the adaptive variance scaling, causing weights with large gradients to be regularized less effectively [10]. Their fix—AdamW (Adam with Decoupled Weight Decay)—
applies weight decay directly to the parameters outside the adaptive gradient step: θt+1 = θt - η λ θt - η m̂ t / (√(v̂ t) + ε) [10]. Today, AdamW is the standard optimizer for training Transformers
across language, vision, and multimodal domains.

A fixed learning rate rarely works across an entire training run. At step zero, random weights produce huge, erratic gradients; taking a large step immediately can cause numerical divergence. Modern recipes therefore begin with a linear warmup—ramping η smoothly from zero to a peak value over the first few hundred or thousand steps—followed by a cosine annealing (or warmup-stable-decay) schedule that gradually lowers η toward a small minimum so the optimizer can settle into fine-grained minima late in training.
To prevent networks from memorizing noise or destabilizing during deep propagation, engineers layer multiple regularization and stabilization mechanisms:
Weight decay: Penalizes excessively large parameter magnitudes, favoring smoother decision boundaries [10].

Dropout: Introduced by Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov in 2014, dropout randomly zeroes out a fraction of hidden units during each training step, preventing neurons from co-adapting and approximating an ensemble of exponentially many thinned sub-networks at test time [4].

Normalization layers: Batch Normalization (common in convolutional networks) and Layer Normalization or RMSNorm (standard in Transformers) rescale intermediate activations to maintain stable mean and variance across deep stacks of layers. Gradient clipping: Caps the global L2 norm of the gradient vector (commonly at 1.0) so
occasional corrupted batches or sharp loss cliffs do not trigger catastrophic "loss spikes" that destroy weeks of progress.

blocks.text: Scaling Up: Distributed Training and Accelerator Hardware

blocks.html: A single modern GPU with 80 GB of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) cannot even hold the optimizer states of a 70-billion-parameter model, let alone train a 405-billion-parameter network on trillions of tokens in a human lifetime. Training at contemporary scale is fundamentally a distributed systems engineering problem.

blocks.text: The Memory Wall and Multi-Dimensional Parallelism

blocks.html: During AdamW mixed-precision training, each model parameter requires memory not just for its working weight, but also for its gradient, a full-precision (FP32) master weight copy, and two FP32 optimizer moments—roughly 16 bytes per parameter before accounting for cached activations [15]. A 100-billion-parameter model thus demands roughly 1.6 terabytes (TB) of

memory solely for model states. To break through single-chip limits, distributed training frameworks combine three orthogonal forms of parallelism—often termed 3D parallelism— plus context/sequence parallelism for long inputs:

1. Data Parallelism & ZeRO / FSDP: Every accelerator holds a copy of the model, processes a different slice of the global mini-batch, and synchronizes gradients via collective all-reduce operations. Standard data parallelism wastes memory by duplicating optimizer states and weights on every chip. In 2019–2020, Microsoft Research introduced ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer), which partitions optimizer states (Stage 1), gradients (Stage 2), and model parameters (Stage 3) across data-parallel workers, gathering parameters on demand during forward and backward passes and cutting per-device memory linearly with cluster size [15]. PyTorch's Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) implements this same sharding paradigm.

2. Tensor Parallelism (Intra-Layer Model Parallelism): Pioneered at scale by NVIDIA's Megatron-LM in 2019, tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices inside each Transformer layer— partitioning the first multi-layer perceptron (MLP) matrix column-wise and the second row-wise, and splitting attention heads across GPUs [14]. Because every layer requires high-speed synchronization (all-reduce) of partial activations, tensor parallelism is typically confined within a single server node linked by ultra-fast interconnects such as NVLink.

3. Pipeline Parallelism (Inter-Layer Model Parallelism): Introduced in Google's GPipe library in 2019, pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive groups of layers to different accelerators, like stations on an assembly line [12]. To avoid leaving downstream chips idle ("pipeline bubbles"), GPipe splits each mini-batch into smaller micro-batches that stream continuously through the pipeline stages, using activation recomputation (checkpointing) to curb memory overhead [12].

blocks.html: Deep learning training is dominated by dense matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMMs). General-purpose CPUs devote much of their silicon die to branch prediction, complex instruction scheduling, and deep cache hierarchies optimized for low-latency serial tasks. By contrast, GPUs (such as NVIDIA's Hopper H100 and Blackwell architectures) and application-specific Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) dedicate massive silicon area to parallel arithmetic arrays— Tensor Cores on GPUs and systolic arrays on TPUs—paired with ultra-high-bandwidth HBM memory.

Google's TPU v4 architecture, detailed by Norman Jouppi and colleagues in April 2023, illustrates how hardware co-design shapes modern training [23]. A TPU v4 supercomputer connects 4,096 chips using dynamically reconfigurable optical circuit switches (OCSes) that let engineers reshape the physical 3D torus interconnect topology on the fly to match a model's parallelism layout and route around failed nodes [23]. Compared to TPU v3, TPU v4
delivered a 2.1× performance gain and 2.7× better performance per watt, while optical switching components accounted for less than 5% of system cost and under 3% of system power [23].

blocks.text: Mixed-Precision Arithmetic: FP32, FP16, BF16, and FP8

blocks.html: Historically, scientific computing defaulted to 32-bit single-precision floating-point arithmetic (FP32). Yet neural networks are remarkably resilient to reduced numerical precision during forward and backward matrix multiplications, provided sensitive accumulations remain accurate. Dropping bit width doubles memory bandwidth efficiency and lets hardware tensor cores execute far more operations per second.

In 2017, Paulius Micikevicius and colleagues formalized mixed-precision training using IEEE 754 16-bit floating point (FP16) for weights, activations, and gradients, while maintaining an FP32 master copy of weights for updates and applying loss scaling to stop tiny gradient values from underflowing to zero [9]. Because FP16 uses only 5 exponent bits, its narrow
dynamic range still caused overflow and instability in very large language models.

The industry largely shifted to BFloat16 (BF16)—Brain Floating Point—validated comprehensively by Dhiraj Kalamkar and colleagues in May 2019 [13]. BF16 allocates 8 exponent bits (matching FP32's exact dynamic range) and 7 mantissa bits, eliminating the need for loss scaling while matching FP32 convergence with identical hyperparameters [13].

The frontier has now moved to 8-bit floating point (FP8). In September 2022, researchers from NVIDIA, Arm, and Intel proposed two complementary FP8 formats: E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) for higher precision in forward weights and activations, and E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits) for wider dynamic range in backward gradients [21]. By late

2024, DeepSeek-V3 demonstrated full-scale FP8 mixed-precision pre-training on a 671-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model across 14.8 trillion tokens using fine-grained tile- and block-wise scaling without a single irrecoverable loss spike [27].

blocks.text: Post-Training: Turning Raw Models into Useful Systems

blocks.html: A base language model that finishes self-supervised pre-training is a powerful next-token predictor, not a reliable assistant. Prompted with a question, it may answer—or it may generate three more questions in the style of a web forum, hallucinate confidently, or reproduce toxic text from its corpus. Transforming a raw pre-trained foundation model into a helpful, safe, instruction-following system requires post-training.

Post-training begins with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), where the model is trained via standard cross-entropy loss on a much smaller, carefully curated dataset of prompt-response demonstrations written by human experts or verified synthetic pipelines. SFT teaches the model conversational formatting, tool invocation syntax, and domain-specific conventions. Yet SFT alone only imitates demonstrations; it does not directly teach the model to distinguish subtle differences between a merely adequate answer and an accurate, well-calibrated one.
To bridge that gap, OpenAI's 2022 InstructGPT paper (Long Ouyang and colleagues) popularized a three-stage RLHF pipeline [19]:
1. Fine-tune the pre-trained model on human-written demonstrations (SFT).
2. Sample multiple responses from the SFT model for a set of prompts, have human labelers rank them from best to worst, and train a separate reward model to predict human preference scores.

3. Optimize the language model policy using PPO to maximize the reward model's score, constrained by a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence penalty that prevents the policy from drifting too far from the SFT reference model and gaming the reward function [19].

The behavioral leap was dramatic: human evaluators preferred outputs from a 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model over the 100× larger 175-billion-parameter base GPT-3 model, while also observing improvements in truthfulness and reductions in toxic output [19].

Traditional PPO-based RLHF is notoriously finicky: it requires hosting multiple large models in memory simultaneously (policy, reference, reward, and value/critic networks) and tuning brittle RL hyperparameters. In May 2023, Rafael Rafailov and colleagues at Stanford introduced Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [24]. By mathematically reparameterizing the closed-form relationship between the optimal RL policy and the underlying reward function, DPO eliminates both the explicit reward model and the online RL sampling loop, optimizing human preferences directly via a simple binary cross-entropy classification loss over preferred (yw) and rejected (yl) response pairs [24]. Meta adopted iterative rounds of SFT, rejection sampling, and DPO to post-train its Llama 3 models [26].

A major post-training shift emerged in 2024–2025: applying large-scale reinforcement learning directly against verifiable, rule-based rewards—such as whether a mathematical proof reaches the exact answer or whether generated code passes unit tests—rather than relying solely on subjective human preference rankings. In January 2025, DeepSeek-AI published DeepSeek-R1, showing that pure reinforcement learning (using Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, which estimates baselines from groups of sampled outputs without a separate critic network) incentivized models to spontaneously develop extended chain-of-thought reasoning, self-verification, and backtracking [28]. DeepSeek-R1 achieved 79.8% Pass@1 on the AIME 2024 mathematics competition, 97.3% on MATH-500, and a 2,029 Elo rating on Codeforces—outperforming 96.3% of human competition participants [28].

blocks.text: Real-World Applications and Industry Case Studies

blocks.html: Abstract principles come into sharpest focus when examining how landmark production systems were actually trained. Four canonical case studies illustrate the breadth of modern training—from scientific discovery to frontier language modeling.

blocks.text: Case Study 1: AlphaFold 2 and Scientific Domain Inductive Bias

blocks.html: Predicting a protein's three-dimensional atomic structure solely from its one-dimensional amino acid sequence had stood as a 50-year grand challenge in biology. In July 2021, John Jumper and colleagues at DeepMind published AlphaFold 2 in Nature [18]. Rather than

throwing a generic off-the-shelf Transformer at raw sequences, the team embedded physical, geometric, and evolutionary knowledge directly into both the architecture (the Evoformer and Structure Module) and the training recipe.

AlphaFold 2 was trained on experimentally determined structures from the Protein Data Bank alongside self-distillation—where an earlier version of the network predicted structures for roughly 350,000 unlabeled sequences, filtered for high confidence, and fed them back into training—paired with a specialized Frame Aligned Point Error (FAPE) geometric loss [18]. At the 14th Critical Assessment of Protein Structure Prediction (CASP14), AlphaFold 2 achieved a median backbone accuracy of 0.96 Å (0.096 nm) root-mean-square deviation across 95% of residues—competitive with experimental X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy [18]. The lesson for practitioners is clear: domain-specific data representations and physics-
aware loss functions can unlock breakthroughs that raw scale alone cannot.

blocks.text: Case Study 2: Scaling Laws and the Chinchilla Reset

blocks.html: How should an organization divide a fixed multi-million-dollar compute budget between building a larger model (N parameters) and feeding it more training data (D tokens)? For a dense Transformer, training compute scales approximately as C ≈ 6ND FLOPs [16]. In January

2020, Jared Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI published empirical power-law scaling laws showing that cross-entropy loss decreases predictably over more than seven orders of magnitude in compute, model size, and dataset size, initially concluding that compute budgets should favor scaling model size much faster than token count [16].

In March 2022, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind revisited that conclusion by training over 400 language models while properly tuning the learning rate schedule to each run's exact token horizon [20]. Their Chinchilla paper revealed that earlier giant models had

been severely under-trained: for training-compute optimality, parameter count and training tokens should scale in roughly equal proportion—approximately 20 tokens per parameter [20]. To prove it, they trained the 70-billion-parameter Chinchilla model on 1.4 trillion tokens using the same compute budget as DeepMind's 280-billion-parameter Gopher (trained on 300 billion tokens). Chinchilla outperformed Gopher across nearly every benchmark, reaching 67.6% five-shot accuracy on MMLU versus Gopher's 60.0%, while being four times smaller to serve [20].

Subsequent industry practice pushed the insight one step further: inference-aware overtraining. Chinchilla minimizes training compute, but a popular model is trained once and queried billions of times. Consequently, labs deliberately train smaller models far past the 20-tokens-per-parameter ratio—for example, training 8-billion-parameter models on 15 trillion tokens (nearly 1,900 tokens per parameter)—trading extra upfront training cost for dramatically cheaper, faster deployment [26].

blocks.text: Case Study 3: Llama 3 405B and Industrial Cluster Reliability

blocks.html: Meta's Llama 3 405B technical report (released July 2024, revised November 2024) offers one of the most transparent engineering accounts of frontier dense-model training [26]. Meta pre-
trained its 405-billion-parameter flagship on 15.6 trillion multilingual, code, and reasoning tokens using 3.8 × 1025 FLOPs across a cluster of 16,384 NVIDIA H100 GPUs [26].

At that scale, hardware failure is not an edge case; it is a daily routine. Over a 54-day pre-training window, the 16,384-GPU job experienced 466 unexpected interruptions—roughly one every three hours—driven primarily by faulty GPUs, HBM memory errors, and networking or host failures [26]. Keeping effective training uptime above 90% required automated fault detection, rapid node eviction, asynchronous checkpointing, and careful 4D parallelism (combining tensor, pipeline, context, and FSDP data parallelism) [26].

blocks.text: Case Study 4: DeepSeek-V3 and Algorithmic Efficiency

blocks.html: While Llama 3 405B demonstrated dense-model engineering at massive cluster scale, DeepSeek-V3 (published December 2024) showcased how architectural sparsity and low-precision numerics compress training budgets [27]. DeepSeek-V3 is a Mixture-of-Experts
(MoE) model with 671 billion total parameters, of which only 37 billion are activated for any single token [27]. Combined with Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), an auxiliary-loss-free

expert load-balancing mechanism, multi-token prediction, and native FP8 mixed-precision training, DeepSeek-V3 completed full training—including pre-training on 14.8 trillion tokens, context extension, and post-training—in 2.788 million NVIDIA H800 GPU hours, without a single irrecoverable loss spike or rollback [27].

Modern machine learning training has transformed pattern recognition, scientific simulation, and natural language interfaces, yet its successes expose hard physical, statistical, and governance constraints.

End-to-end representation learning excels wherever rules are too intricate, noisy, or high-dimensional to codify manually—from acoustic speech variations to protein folding and multimodal perception. Once trained, foundation models amortize their upfront compute across thousands of downstream tasks via fine-tuning or in-context prompting.

Yet trained models inherit deep limitations. They are statistical approximators, not infallible reasoning engines; they remain vulnerable to distribution shift when deployment data diverges from training distributions, can hallucinate plausible falsehoods, and encode historical biases present in human-generated corpora. Moreover, debugging a trained neural network is fundamentally harder than debugging source code: when a model fails on an edge case, engineers cannot simply edit line 42 of a script—they must diagnose data gaps, adjust reward signals, or retrain while guarding against regressions elsewhere.

The physical footprint of training and serving large models has moved from a niche engineering concern to a macroeconomic infrastructure issue. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA)'s April 2025 Energy and AI report, global data centers consumed an estimated 415 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, roughly 1.5% of global electricity consumption [29]. In its April 2026 flagship update, Key Questions on Energy and AI, the IEA

reported that global data center electricity consumption climbed to approximately 485 TWh in 2025—and projected it to roughly double to 950 TWh by 2030, representing around 3% of global electricity demand [30]. While accelerated servers drive the steepest share of that

growth, physical bottlenecks in grid interconnection queues, transformer manufacturing, and local cooling capacity are increasingly constraining where and how fast massive training clusters can be built [29] [30].

Frontier models now ingest tens of trillions of tokens—approaching the practical ceiling of unique, high-quality public human text on the open web. To keep scaling, labs increasingly augment training mixes with synthetic data generated by earlier models. That strategy carries a documented statistical hazard. In July 2024, Ilia Shumailov, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, and Yarin Gal published a landmark study in Nature demonstrating model collapse: when generative models are recursively trained on data produced by previous generations of models, tail events vanish, output variance shrinks, and performance degrades irreversibly into repetitive gibberish [25]. Avoiding collapse requires

preserving fresh human-authored data streams, strict provenance tracking, and filtering synthetic outputs through external verifiers (such as compilers, proof assistants, or physics simulators) rather than naive self-training.

Because training choices lock in safety, privacy, and reliability properties long before deployment, institutional standards now treat training as a lifecycle governance discipline. Published in January 2023, the National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) organizes risk controls across four functions—Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage—emphasizing dataset provenance, adversarial testing, bias auditing, and continuous monitoring rather than one-off benchmark checks [22].
To evaluate where machine learning training is headed without drifting into hype, it helps to draw a sharp line between established production practices and active research frontiers.

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) as default frontier architecture: Activating only a small fraction of total parameters per token decouples model knowledge capacity from per-token training and inference FLOPs, as validated at scale by DeepSeek-V3 and contemporaries [27].

Sub-16-bit native training: FP8 training with fine-grained scaling factors has moved from academic proposal to production reality, cutting memory bandwidth pressure and boosting accelerator throughput [21] [27].

Post-training RL for verifiable reasoning: Rather than treating post-training purely as stylistic alignment, labs now allocate substantial compute to reinforcement learning against verifiable math, coding, and tool-use environments, dramatically expanding multi-step problem solving [28].

Inference-aware overtraining: Training compact models far beyond the classic Chinchilla 20-tokens-per-parameter ratio is now standard practice for lowering serving latency and enabling edge deployment [20] [26].

Ultra-low-precision and microscaling formats (FP4 / MXFP): Hardware and algorithmic research is actively testing 4-bit floating-point training and microscaling block formats; whether these can match BF16/FP8 stability across all frontier modalities without fragile tuning remains an open engineering question. Decentralized and geographically distributed training: Because single-site power availability is tightening, researchers are exploring low-communication training algorithms (such as local-SGD variants and asynchronous gradient compression) capable of spanning multiple data centers connected over standard wide-area networks.

Continual and online learning: Today's models remain largely frozen snapshots of their training cutoff. Developing training algorithms that safely incorporate new knowledge in real time— without catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills or vulnerability to data poisoning—remains one of machine learning's hardest unsolved problems. Automated scientific and formal-verification data loops: As web text saturates, future training gains may depend less on scraping larger human corpora and more on closed-loop environments—automated laboratories, code sandboxes, and formal theorem provers—that generate ground-truth feedback at machine speed without triggering model collapse.

blocks.text: Conclusion: The Craft Beneath the Compute

blocks.html: It is tempting to view modern machine learning training as a brute-force exercise in stacking GPUs and pouring terabytes of internet text into an opaque mathematical furnace. Look closer, and a different picture emerges. Every reliable model is the cumulative product of deliberate engineering decisions: how raw observations are filtered and tokenized, how an objective function encodes what matters, how an optimizer navigates billion-dimensional curvature without diverging, how thousands of chips stay synchronized through daily hardware failures, and how post-training aligns raw statistical capability with human intent and verifiable truth.

As hardware architectures evolve and energy constraints tighten, the organizations that build the most capable systems will not simply be those with the largest clusters—they will be the teams that master every link in the training pipeline, turning finite data and finite power into durable, trustworthy intelligence.

1. What is the difference between training and inference in machine learning? Training is the iterative process of adjusting a model's internal weights using data, a loss function, and an optimizer (such as AdamW) so the model learns patterns; it requires both forward and backward passes and consumes massive compute and memory. Inference is the deployment phase, where the trained weights are frozen and the model executes only forward passes to generate predictions or responses on new inputs.

2. How long does it take to train a large machine learning model? Training duration ranges from seconds on a laptop for tabular decision trees or small classifiers to several months on supercomputing clusters for frontier foundation models. For example, Meta pre-trained its 405-billion-parameter Llama 3 model over 54 days on 16,384 NVIDIA H100 GPUs [26],
whereas DeepSeek-V3 completed its full training pipeline in 2.788 million H800 GPU hours [27].

3. Why do modern AI models rely on self-supervised learning instead of supervised learning for pre-training? Supervised learning requires human-verified labels for every example, which becomes prohibitively expensive at web scale. Self-supervised learning generates targets automatically from raw unlabeled data—such as predicting the next token in text or matching augmented views of an image—allowing models to learn broad representations from trillions of tokens before specialized fine-tuning [11] [17].

4. What are epochs, batches, and learning rates? A batch (or mini-batch) is the subset of training examples processed together before computing an average gradient and updating weights. An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset. The learning rate controls the step size of each weight update; schedules typically warm it up gradually at the start of training and decay it toward zero near the end for stable convergence.

5. Why is mixed-precision training (BF16 and FP8) used instead of standard FP32? Standard 32-bit floating-point arithmetic (FP32) consumes twice the memory bandwidth of 16-bit formats and four times that of 8-bit formats. Mixed-precision training performs bulk matrix multiplications in BF16 or FP8—dramatically increasing hardware throughput and shrinking memory footprints—while keeping sensitive master weights and optimizer states in FP32 to preserve numerical stability [9] [13] [21].

6. What is the difference between RLHF and DPO in post-training? Both align a pre-trained model with human preferences. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) trains a separate reward model on human rankings and then uses an online RL algorithm like PPO to optimize the language model against that reward [19]. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
mathematically eliminates the separate reward model and RL sampling loop, optimizing preferred versus rejected response pairs directly through a simpler classification loss [24].

7. What are the Chinchilla scaling laws, and do labs still follow them? Published by DeepMind in 2022, the Chinchilla scaling laws showed that minimizing pre-training loss for a fixed compute budget requires scaling model parameters and training tokens equally—at roughly 20 tokens per parameter [20]. While this remains the baseline for training-compute optimality,

many production labs deliberately "overtrain" smaller models on far more than 20 tokens per parameter because smaller models are much cheaper and faster to run during billions of real-world inference queries [26].

8. What is model collapse, and why does it matter for synthetic training data? Model collapse is a statistical degradation documented in a 2024 Nature study by Shumailov et al., occurring when generative models are recursively trained on data generated by earlier AI models [25]. Over successive generations, rare patterns disappear and errors compound,
causing outputs to lose diversity and accuracy. Teams mitigate it by retaining fresh human data and filtering synthetic examples through objective external verifiers.

blocks.html: Every time a smartphone recalculates a highway detour in under a second, a hospital triage dashboard flags a high-risk patient, or a language model drafts a legal clause, a quiet choreography of mathematical instructions unfolds inside silicon. Public conversation often treats "the algorithm" as a singular, opaque force steering social feeds or credit decisions. In computer science, the reality is both simpler and more profound. An algorithm is not a mystical black box; it is a finite, unambiguous recipe for transforming an input into a desired output.

Yet that modest definition conceals a dramatic transformation. For more than two thousand years, algorithms were deterministic procedures crafted line by line by human minds—exact sequences of arithmetic, comparisons, and branches whose behavior could be proved on paper before a single calculation ran. Over the past two decades, a second class of computation has moved to the center of technology: statistical and learned systems whose internal rules are not written directly by programmers, but induced from vast datasets through optimization. Even more recently, reinforcement learning agents and evolutionary coding systems have begun discovering faster classical algorithms than human engineers had found in half a century [17], [18], [20].

To understand modern artificial intelligence—how models learn, why they fail, and where their mathematical limits lie—one has to start beneath the neural layers, with the theory and craft of algorithms themselves.

blocks.text: From Euclid's Compass to Turing's Tape: A Historical Arc

blocks.html: Long before electronic circuits existed, mathematicians recognized that solving a problem once was less valuable than specifying a reliable method that solved every instance of that problem. Around 300 BCE, the Greek geometer Euclid recorded one of the oldest surviving numerical procedures in Book VII of his Elements: a method for finding the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two positive integers by repeatedly replacing the larger number with the remainder of dividing it by the smaller until the remainder reaches zero. More than two millennia later, variations of the Euclidean algorithm still sit inside cryptographic libraries and computer algebra systems.

The word "algorithm" itself arrived over a millennium later, born from a translation quirk. Around 820 CE, working at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, the Persian polymath Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi authored foundational treatises on linear and quadratic equations (Hisab al-jabr w'al-muqabala, which gave us the word "algebra") and on calculation with Hindu-Arabic positional numerals [1]. When his arithmetic treatise was translated into Latin in the twelfth century under the title Algoritmi de Numero Indorum ("Algoritmi on the Hindu Art of Reckoning"), European scholars adopted "Algoritmi"—the Latinized rendering of al-Khwarizmi's name—and turned it into "algorism" for decimal arithmetic, and eventually "algorithm" for any systematic computational procedure [1].

For centuries, algorithms were executed exclusively by human "computers" armed with ink, paper, and astronomical tables. The conceptual leap toward mechanical execution came in the nineteenth century. In 1843, Ada Lovelace published her English translation of Italian military engineer Luigi Federico Menabrea's memoir on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine —a steam-powered, programmable mechanical computer that was never completed in Babbage's lifetime [2]. Lovelace appended seven extensive notes, longer than Menabrea's

original paper. In Note G, she laid out a step-by-step operational table—complete with variables, intermediate registers, and iterative loops—for computing the sequence of Bernoulli numbers on the machine [2]. Equally prescient was her observation that a general-purpose

engine need not be restricted to numbers: if the fundamental relationships of music or symbolic logic could be expressed as abstract operations, the machine could manipulate them as readily as arithmetic [2].

What remained missing in 1843 was a rigorous mathematical definition of what "computable" actually meant. That question became urgent in 1928, when German mathematician David Hilbert posed the Entscheidungsproblem (decision problem): could there exist a single mechanical procedure capable of deciding, for any statement in first-order logic, whether that statement is universally valid?

In 1936, two mathematicians answered in the negative using radically different formalisms. At Princeton, Alonzo Church introduced the lambda calculus, a system of symbolic function abstraction and substitution. Across the Atlantic, 24-year-old Alan Turing submitted his landmark paper, "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem," published in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society in late 1936 [3]. Turing

stripped computation down to its barest physical metaphor: an idealized machine equipped with an infinite tape divided into squares, a read-write head that inspects one symbol at a time, and a finite table of state-transition rules [3].

Turing proved two results that still anchor computer science. First, he constructed a "universal computing machine"—a single Turing machine that could read the encoded description of any other Turing machine from its tape and simulate it, establishing the theoretical blueprint for the stored-program digital computer [3]. Second, he proved that certain well-defined problems
are fundamentally unsolvable by any algorithm—most famously the halting problem, which asks whether an arbitrary program will eventually finish running or loop forever [3]. Soon after,

Church and Turing showed their formalisms were mathematically equivalent, giving rise to the Church-Turing thesis: the foundational principle that any computation achievable by an effective, step-by-step mechanical method—requiring finite instructions and no human intuition—can be executed by a Turing machine [4].

blocks.text: What Makes an Algorithm: Formal Definitions and Computational Complexity

blocks.html: With the boundaries of computability mapped out, computer scientists turned to the engineering question: what distinguishes a genuine algorithm from a vague heuristic, and how do we measure whether an algorithm is fast enough to be useful?
In the first volume of his encyclopedic The Art of Computer Programming, Stanford computer scientist Donald Knuth distilled five formal properties that every true algorithm must satisfy [5]:

1. Finiteness: The procedure must always terminate after a finite number of steps. A set of rules that runs indefinitely without halting is a computational process (such as an operating system kernel), not an algorithm in the strict sense.
2. Definiteness: Every step must be specified with complete precision, leaving zero ambiguity about what action to perform next.
3. Input: The procedure accepts zero or more well-defined inputs drawn from specified sets of objects before or during execution.
4. Output: It produces one or more outputs bearing a specified mathematical relationship to the inputs.
5. Effectiveness: Every operation must be basic enough that it can, in principle, be performed exactly and in finite time by a mechanical agent using finite resources.

Knowing that an algorithm terminates, however, offers cold comfort if it finishes after the heat death of the universe. To compare algorithms independently of clock speeds, compiler quirks, or programming languages, computer scientists rely on asymptotic analysis—measuring how an algorithm's resource consumption (execution time or memory space) grows as the input size n becomes arbitrarily large.

Asymptotic notation originated in nineteenth-century number theory with Paul Bachmann (1894) and Edmund Landau (1909), before Donald Knuth standardized its modern computer science usage in a 1976 ACM SIGACT News paper [6]. Three symbols do most of the analytical
heavy lifting:

Big-O notation, O(f(n)), expresses an asymptotic upper bound. Formally, a function T(n) is O(f(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n<sub>0</sub> such that 0 ≤ T(n) ≤ c · f(n) for all n ≥ n<sub>0</sub>. It captures the
worst-case growth ceiling. Big-Omega notation, Ω(f(n)), expresses an asymptotic lower bound: T(n) ≥ c · f(n) for all sufficiently large n, establishing the minimum work required.
Big-Theta notation, Θ(f(n)), denotes a tight bound, meaning T(n) grows at the exact same asymptotic rate as f(n) from both above and below [6].

Because asymptotic notation strips away constant multipliers and lower-order terms—treating 5n<sup>2</sup> + 120n + 8 simply as O(n<sup>2</sup>)—it isolates the structural scaling behavior that dominates at real-world data sizes. The gap between complexity classes is not merely academic; it separates instantaneous software from physical impossibility.

Time is only half the ledger. Every algorithm also negotiates a time-space tradeoff: storing precomputed intermediate results in memory (RAM) can dramatically slash execution time, while operating under tight memory ceilings often forces repeated recomputation. Hash tables trade extra memory slots for O(1) average lookup times; modern road-routing engines precompute millions of shortcut edges into gigabytes of graph indices so live route queries finish in microseconds [12].

At the deepest layer of complexity theory lies the P versus NP problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems designated by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, carrying a $1 million reward for a proof [8]. The class P (polynomial time) comprises decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in $O(n^k)$ time for some constant $k$—problems generally regarded as computationally tractable. The class NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) comprises decision problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding a solution from scratch appears to require exponential search [8].

In May 1971, Stephen Cook proved in "The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures" that Boolean satisfiability (SAT)—determining whether variables in a logical formula can be assigned true or false to make the whole formula true—is NP-complete: any problem in NP can be reduced to SAT in polynomial time [7]. Leonid Levin proved an equivalent result

independently in the Soviet Union, and Richard Karp demonstrated in 1972 that 21 classic combinatorial problems—including the traveling salesman decision problem, graph coloring, and knapsack packing—share this exact NP-complete core [8].

The consequence is stark: if anyone discovers a polynomial-time algorithm for a single NP-complete problem, then P = NP, and thousands of seemingly intractable optimization, scheduling, and logistics puzzles collapse into tractability overnight. Conversely, if P ≠ NP—as most theoretical computer scientists conjecture—then hard combinatorial problems possess an intrinsic mathematical barrier that no clever deterministic algorithm can bypass, forcing engineers to rely on approximation algorithms, heuristics, or learned models.

blocks.text: The Classical Toolkit: Core Algorithmic Paradigms

blocks.html: Over seven decades of computer science, engineers have distilled recurring problem-solving patterns into a handful of foundational paradigms. Rather than memorizing thousands of isolated procedures, algorithm designers match the mathematical structure of a problem to the paradigm best suited to exploit it.

Divide-and-conquer breaks a large problem into smaller, independent subproblems of the same type, solves each recursively, and merges the partial answers. Sorting provides the textbook example: Merge sort splits an array of length n in half repeatedly until reaching single elements, then merges sorted halves in linear time, achieving a guaranteed worst-case runtime of Θ(n log n).

Divide-and-conquer can also overturn long-held assumptions about arithmetic itself. Multiplying two n × n matrices using the textbook row-by-column definition requires n3 scalar multiplications—eight multiplications for a 2 × 2 block. In 1969, German mathematician Volker Strassen stunned numerical analysts by publishing a three-page paper, "Gaussian Elimination is not Optimal," showing that two 2 × 2 matrices can be multiplied using only seven scalar multiplications combined with extra additions [9]. Applied recursively, Strassen's algorithm drops asymptotic matrix multiplication complexity from O(n3) to O(nlog2 7) ≈ O(n2.807) [9]. That
single insight launched a half-century quest to drive down the matrix multiplication exponent \omega, a race that directly underpins modern deep learning hardware.

When subproblems are not independent—when a naive recursion solves the exact same subproblem over and over—divide-and-conquer wastes exponential effort. Dynamic programming, formalized by mathematician Richard Bellman in the 1950s, solves problems exhibiting two properties: optimal substructure (an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems) and overlapping subproblems. By storing each subproblem's solution in a table (memoization or bottom-up tabulation), dynamic programming converts exponential tree searches into polynomial-time passes. Sequence alignment in genomics (the Needleman-Wunsch and Smith-Waterman algorithms), shortest-path routing with negative weights (Bellman-Ford), and speech recognition decoding (the Viterbi algorithm) all rely on dynamic programming.

A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping that a sequence of myopic best decisions yields a globally optimal result. For many problems, greedy logic fails— taking the cheapest flight leg out of a hub can trap you on an expensive connection later. Yet for problems with a specific mathematical structure (known as matroids or problems with the greedy-choice property), greedy methods are both remarkably fast and provably optimal. David Huffman's 1952 prefix-coding algorithm builds minimum-redundancy lossless compression trees greedily by merging the two least-frequent symbols at each step; Joseph Kruskal's and Robert Prim's algorithms construct minimum spanning trees across weighted networks using greedy edge selection.

Graphs—collections of vertices (nodes) connected by weighted edges—model everything from fiber-optic backbones to social networks and molecular bonds. In 1959, Dutch computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra published "A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs," introducing an algorithm that finds the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a graph with non-negative edge weights [10]. Using a priority queue (such as a binary or
Fibonacci heap), Dijkstra's algorithm expands outward from the origin in waves of strictly increasing cumulative distance, guaranteeing optimality once the target node is settled [10].

Dijkstra's blind outward expansion, however, wastes effort exploring roads heading in the wrong direction. In 1968, Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael at the Stanford Research Institute formalized the A* search algorithm to guide Shakey the Robot across rooms [11]. A* prioritizes candidate nodes by minimizing an evaluation function:

blocks.raw: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)

blocks.html: Here, g(n) is the exact known cost from the start node to node n, and h(n) is a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost from n to the goal (such as straight-line Euclidean distance on a map) [11]. Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael proved that if h(n) is admissible—meaning it never overestimates the true remaining cost—A* is guaranteed to find the optimal shortest path while expanding no more nodes than any other equally informed optimal search algorithm [11].

blocks.text: Probabilistic Search and Monte Carlo Tree Search

blocks.html: Deterministic search breaks down when branching factors explode. In the ancient board game Go, a 19 × 19 board presents roughly 250 legal moves per turn and more possible board configurations than atoms in the observable universe—far beyond the reach of exhaustive minimax search or simple hand-crafted heuristics.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) tackles vast decision spaces by replacing exhaustive breadth with asymmetric, statistically guided sampling. Across thousands of iterations, MCTS repeats four phases: selection (descending the existing search tree by balancing high-value moves against under-explored moves via an Upper Confidence Bound formula), expansion (adding a new child node), simulation (estimating the node's value through random playouts or a learned evaluator), and backpropagation (updating win-rate statistics up the tree to the root).
In January 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo demonstrated the power of fusing classical MCTS with deep neural networks [13]. Instead of relying on noisy random rollouts alone, AlphaGo used a

policy network to narrow the branching factor to promising moves and a value network to evaluate board positions directly inside the MCTS tree—defeating European champion Fan Hui 5–0 and, two months later, world champion Lee Sedol 4–1 [13].

blocks.text: The Great Inversion: From Hand-Coded Rules to Learned Algorithms

blocks.html: For the first four decades of artificial intelligence research, engineers tried to encode human intelligence using classical symbolic algorithms: explicit if-then production rules, logic programming, and hand-engineered knowledge bases. Expert systems of the 1980s could diagnose specific bacterial infections or configure minicomputer orders, yet they shattered on tasks a five-year-old performs effortlessly—recognizing a handwritten digit in poor lighting, parsing ambiguous spoken grammar, or identifying a pedestrian partially occluded by a parked van. The real world simply contains too many edge cases to enumerate by hand.

Modern machine learning inverted the classical programming paradigm. In traditional software engineering, a human writes the algorithm (rules) and feeds it data to produce answers. In supervised machine learning, a human supplies data and answers (labels), and an optimization algorithm searches a parameterized family of mathematical functions to infer the rules—stored not as readable if/else statements, but as millions or trillions of floating-point weights.

In their landmark May 2015 Nature review, Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey Hinton explained how deep learning—multi-layered neural networks trained via stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation—eliminated the need for hand-crafted feature extractors [14]. By composing simple non-linear transformations across dozens or hundreds of layers, deep networks automatically learn hierarchical representations: raw pixels become edges, edges become textures, textures become object parts, and parts become semantic categories [14]. (For a closer look at how those optimization loops work in practice, see VIZRA's companion guides on How Machine Learning Models Are Trained and Gradient Descent and Backpropagation Explained.)
Two years later, in June 2017, eight researchers at Google published "Attention Is All You Need," introducing the Transformer architecture [15]. Previous sequence models—recurrent

neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks—processed text token by token, creating a sequential bottleneck that prevented efficient parallelization on modern GPUs. The Transformer dispensed with recurrence entirely, replacing it with scaled dot-product self-attention:

blocks.raw:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QKT
√(dk) )V

blocks.html: where Q (queries), K (keys), and V (values) are learned linear projections of the input sequence and dk is the key dimension [15]. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation benchmark,
the Transformer achieved a state-of-the-art 41.8 BLEU score after just 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs, unlocking the scaling laws that birthed today's foundation models [15].

In March 2019, reinforcement learning pioneer Richard Sutton captured the philosophical shift in an influential essay titled "The Bitter Lesson" [16]. Looking back across 70 years of AI—from computer chess and Go to speech recognition and computer vision—Sutton observed that leveraging human domain knowledge often delivers short-term gains, but eventually plateaus and even impedes progress [16]. Over the long run, the only two general-purpose algorithmic
methods that continue scaling arbitrarily with Moore's Law and hardware compute are search and learning [16].

Crucially, however, learned models have not replaced classical algorithms—they run on top of them. Training a frontier Transformer requires classical numerical linear algebra (heavily optimized matrix multiplication kernels), automatic differentiation (reverse-mode backpropagation), distributed all-reduce communication algorithms across thousands of accelerators, and classical sampling or beam-search algorithms at inference time. Modern AI is a hybrid stack: classical algorithms provide the deterministic engine that trains and executes statistical models.
