blocks.text: 1. What is the difference between a foundation model and a large language model (LLM)?

blocks.html: Every modern large language model—such as GPT-4, Claude, or Llama 3—is a foundation model, but not every foundation model is an LLM. "Foundation model" is the broader paradigm coined by Stanford CRFM in 2021 for any large-scale, self-supervised base model adaptable across many downstream tasks [1]. LLMs specialize in text and code, whereas non-text foundation models operate on images (CLIP, SAM), speech (Whisper), weather grids (GraphCast), satellite imagery (Prithvi), robotics (RT-2), and biomolecular structures (AlphaFold 3) [5], [6], [9], [10].

blocks.text: 2. Why did Stanford researchers call them "foundation" models instead of "general AI"?

blocks.html: Rishi Bommasani, Percy Liang, and the Stanford CRFM team chose the word foundation specifically to capture their "critically central yet incomplete character" [1]. Unlike Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a foundation model is not an autonomous, finished intelligence; it is an architectural substrate that must be adapted, grounded, and wrapped in safety and software controls to serve specific downstream tasks.

blocks.text: 3. Are emergent abilities in foundation models real or a measurement artifact?

blocks.html: Both views capture part of the picture. In 2022, Wei et al. documented capabilities that appeared suddenly once models passed certain size thresholds [13]. In 2023, Schaeffer et al.
showed that many of those sharp jumps smooth out into predictable curves when evaluated with continuous metrics instead of all-or-nothing exact-match scores [14]. Even when
underlying statistical loss improves smoothly, however, real-world usability often crosses practical competence thresholds abruptly.

blocks.text: 4. When should an organization use RAG versus fine-tuning (or LoRA)?

blocks.html: Use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) when the model needs up-to-date, proprietary, or verifiable factual information without modifying its weights [17]. Use fine-tuning—especially

parameter-efficient methods like LoRA—when you need to change how the model behaves, such as enforcing a specialized output schema, adopting a domain-specific tone, or improving accuracy on a narrow technical task [16]. Many enterprise deployments combine both.

blocks.text: 5. What is the difference between "open-weight" and "open-source" foundation models?

blocks.html: An open-weight model (such as Llama 3 or Mixtral 8×7B) publicly releases its trained neural parameters so developers can download, host, and fine-tune it on their own hardware [19], [22]. True open-source AI would also publish the complete pretraining datasets, data-curation
scripts, and full training code under an OSI-approved license—a much higher bar that very few frontier models meet.

blocks.text: 6. How much energy do foundation models and AI data centers consume?

blocks.html: According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global data centers consumed roughly 415 TWh of electricity in 2024—about 1.5% of worldwide electricity demand—and grew by 17% in 2025 [27], [27]. While AI is only part of total data center load, hyperscale AI-focused facilities
now routinely draw 100 MW or more, compared with 10 to 25 MW for conventional data centers [27].

blocks.text: 7. How does the EU AI Act regulate foundation models?

blocks.html: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) regulates foundation models as General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models, with core obligations applicable since August 2, 2025 [31]. All GPAI

providers must maintain technical documentation, follow EU copyright policies, and publish a training-data summary. Models presumed to carry systemic risk—defined under Article 51 as exceeding 1025 FLOPs of training compute—must also undergo adversarial testing, risk mitigation, cybersecurity hardening, and serious-incident reporting [31].

blocks.text: 8. Why is homogenization considered both the biggest strength and biggest risk of foundation models?

blocks.html: Homogenization allows one breakthrough in a base model to upgrade thousands of downstream applications simultaneously [1]. Conversely, it creates monoculture risk: any bias,
hallucination tendency, or security exploit embedded in the shared foundation is automatically inherited by every downstream product built upon it.

title: Understanding Transformers: The Architecture Behind Modern AI
deck: In June 2017, eight Google researchers stripped recurrence out of neural networks and replaced it with pure attention. Nearly a decade later, that single architectural bet underpins large language models, protein folding, speech recognition, and generative video—even as engineers push against its quadratic limits with hardware-aware kernels, sparse experts, and hybrid state-space designs.

Nearly a decade later, that single architectural bet underpins large language models, protein folding, speech recognition, and generative video—even as engineers push against its quadratic limits with hardware-aware kernels, sparse experts, and hybrid state-space designs.

blocks.text: The Architecture That Swallowed Artificial Intelligence

blocks.html: In June 2017, eight researchers at Google Brain and Google Research uploaded a fifteen-page paper to arXiv with a title that sounded equal parts manifesto and provocation: Attention Is All You Need [4]. Their immediate target was unglamorous by today's standards—improving automated translation between English, German, and French. Yet buried inside that translation benchmark was a radical structural wager. For two decades, the field had treated sequential data like language as an assembly line, forcing neural networks to read one word after another in strict order. The Google team threw the assembly line away. They removed recurrent loops, discarded convolutional filters, and built a network called the Transformer out of a single core primitive: self-attention [4].

Few engineering bets in computer science have paid off so completely. By 2026, Attention Is All You Need had accumulated more than 150,000 citations, making it one of the most cited scientific papers of the twenty-first century. More telling than the citation count is the architectural monoculture it created. The Transformer did not merely improve translation; it became the common substrate for large language models, code assistants, speech recognizers, image classifiers, video generators, and biomolecular structure predictors. When a software engineer autocompletes a function, a biologist models a protein–ligand complex, or a filmmaker generates a sixty-second video clip from a text prompt, the mathematical engine turning underneath is almost always a recognizable descendant of that 2017 blueprint.

Understanding how Transformers work—and where they strain—is no longer niche knowledge reserved for deep learning researchers. It is the baseline literacy required to evaluate modern artificial intelligence. The architecture's triumph was never about biological realism or human-like cognition. It was about a precise alignment between mathematics and silicon: turning sequence understanding into dense, parallel matrix multiplications that graphics processing units (GPUs) could devour at unprecedented scale. Tracing how that design evolved from a 65-million-parameter translation model into today's trillion-scale sparse networks reveals both why modern AI looks the way it does and what is likely to come next.

To appreciate why the Transformer felt like a jailbreak, you have to look at the prison researchers were trying to escape. Before 2017, the dominant engines for language, speech, and time-series data were recurrent neural networks (RNNs). An RNN processes a sequence step by step: at time step t, it takes the current input token x<sub>t</sub> and combines it with a hidden state h<sub>t-1</sub> carried over from the previous step to produce an updated hidden state h<sub>t</sub>. On paper,
this loop mirrors how humans read a sentence from left to right, updating a mental summary as each word arrives.

In practice, standard RNNs broke down on long sequences. During training, errors must flow backward through every time step via backpropagation through time. Repeatedly multiplying gradients across dozens of steps caused those signals to either shrink toward zero (the vanishing gradient problem) or blow up uncontrollably (the exploding gradient problem). A plain RNN trying to link a subject at the beginning of a paragraph to a verb fifty words later simply forgot the subject.

In 1997, Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed a durable fix: the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network [1]. Rather than overwriting a single hidden vector at every step, an LSTM maintains a separate cell state protected by learned multiplicative gates— mechanisms that decide what new information to admit, what to discard, and what to expose. Seventeen years later, in June 2014, Kyunghyun Cho and colleagues introduced a streamlined variant, the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), inside an RNN Encoder–Decoder framework for machine translation [2]. By merging the cell state and hidden state and using fewer gates, GRUs matched LSTM accuracy on many tasks with lower computational overhead.

Encoder–decoder RNNs powered the first wave of production neural machine translation, but they suffered from two fatal bottlenecks. The first was representational: the encoder had to compress an entire source sentence—whether five words or fifty—into a single fixed-length vector, and the decoder had to reconstruct the entire translation from that lone summary. Performance degraded sharply as sentences grew longer.

In September 2014, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio broke that information bottleneck with the paper Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate [3]. Instead of forcing the encoder to squash the whole sentence into one final

vector, they allowed the decoder to look back at every encoder hidden state at each decoding step. A small learned scoring network—an additive attention mechanism—computed a weighted average of those source states, letting the model dynamically focus on the most relevant input words as it generated each output word [3].

Bahdanau attention dramatically improved translation quality, yet the second bottleneck remained untouched. Because both the encoder and the decoder were still recurrent networks, computing hidden state h<sub>t</sub> strictly required waiting for h<sub>t-1</sub> to finish. You could not

compute all token representations in a sentence simultaneously. That sequential dependency starved modern GPU clusters of parallel work. As datasets swelled into billions of words, researchers were stuck pushing data through a single-file straw.

Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin asked a deceptively simple question: if attention already lets any word look directly at any other word, why keep the recurrent network at all?

Their Transformer architecture replaced recurrence entirely with stacked layers of self-attention and point-wise feed-forward networks [4]. Removing the recurrent loop produced two immediate mathematical wins. First, the maximum path length between any two tokens in a sequence dropped from O(n) sequential steps in an RNN to O(1)—a single attention hop— regardless of whether two related words sat two positions apart or two thousand [4]. Long-
range dependencies no longer had to survive a game of telephone across dozens of intermediate hidden states.

Second, and even more consequential for hardware, every token in a training sequence could now be processed in parallel. Instead of looping sequentially across a sentence, a Transformer packs the entire sequence into matrices and computes all pairwise token interactions in one sweeping matrix multiplication. GPUs are purpose-built for large matrix multiplications.

The empirical results published at NeurIPS 2017 were unmistakable. On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation benchmark, the large Transformer achieved a BLEU score of 28.4, beating the best previously reported models—including multi-model ensembles—by more than 2 BLEU points [4]. On WMT 2014 English-to-French, a single Transformer reached
41.8 BLEU after training for just 3.5 days on eight NVIDIA P100 GPUs, a small fraction of the compute required by competing recurrent and convolutional systems [4]. The original base

model was tiny by modern standards—six encoder layers, six decoder layers, a hidden dimension of 512, and eight attention heads—yet it proved that dropping recurrence did not merely match sequential models; it unlocked an order-of-magnitude leap in training throughput.

blocks.text: Inside the Machine: How a Transformer Works Step by Step

blocks.html: Stripped of hype, a Transformer is a surprisingly clean pipeline of linear algebra, nonlinear activations, and normalization layers. Tracing a single input sentence from raw characters to output probabilities shows how each component solves a specific mathematical problem.

Neural networks cannot multiply words; they multiply floating-point numbers. The pipeline begins with a tokenizer—typically a subword algorithm such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or WordPiece—that slices raw text into discrete units called tokens. Common words like architecture often map to a single token, while rare words or technical compounds split into recognizable subword pieces. This keeps the vocabulary manageable (typically 32,000 to over 128,000 entries in modern models) while ensuring the network never hits an "unknown word" dead end.

Each token ID looks up a row in a learned embedding matrix E ∈ ℝV × dmodel, where V is the vocabulary size and dmodel is the model's internal vector width (512 in the original 2017 base Transformer, scaling to 4,096, 8,192, or 16,384 in frontier models) [4] [26]. In this high-
dimensional space, tokens with related grammatical roles or meanings gradually drift into nearby geometric regions during training.

blocks.text: Positional Encodings: From Sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi

blocks.html: Because self-attention compares every token with every other token simultaneously, it is inherently permutation-equivariant: without extra information, "the dog chased the cat" and "the cat chased the dog" would look like the exact same bag of vectors. Order has to be injected explicitly.
Vaswani et al. solved this by adding fixed sinusoidal positional encodings directly to the token embeddings before the first layer [4]:

blocks.raw:
PE(pos, 2i) = sin(
pos
100002i / dmodel ),    PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(
pos
100002i / dmodel )

blocks.html: Here pos is the token's index in the sequence and i indexes the embedding dimension. Each dimension oscillates at a different geometric wavelength, giving every position a unique fingerprint while allowing relative offsets to be expressed as linear transformations. Early models like BERT and GPT-2 instead used learned absolute positional embedding tables [6]. Both absolute approaches, however, struggled when asked to generalize to sequences longer than those seen during training.

Modern Transformers largely replaced additive absolute encodings with two relative-position methods. The dominant choice across open-weight and frontier language models—including Meta's Llama series, Mistral, and DeepSeek—is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), introduced by Jianlin Su and colleagues in April 2021 [12]. Rather than adding a position vector

to token embeddings at the input, RoPE rotates each token's query and key vectors in two-dimensional subspaces by an angle proportional to its position m. When the model takes the dot product between a query at position m and a key at position n, the geometry of rotation ensures the result depends naturally on the relative distance m - n, while exhibiting a gradual long-term decay as tokens move farther apart [12].

An influential alternative is Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi), proposed by Ofir Press, Noah A. Smith, and Mike Lewis in August 2021 [13]. ALiBi removes positional embeddings from the input altogether. Instead, it subtracts a static, non-learned linear penalty proportional to token distance directly from the query–key attention scores, with different attention heads using different penalty slopes. Press et al. demonstrated that a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained on 1,024-token sequences with ALiBi could extrapolate to 2,048-token sequences at inference time with the same perplexity as a sinusoidal model trained natively on 2,048 tokens—while training 11% faster and using 11% less memory [13].

blocks.text: Scaled Dot-Product Attention and Q/K/V Projections

blocks.html: At the core of every Transformer block sits scaled dot-product attention [4]. Imagine

searching a vast reference library. You arrive with a specific question (a Query), scan the index labels on every folder in the room (the Keys), and pull out a weighted blend of the actual contents inside the best-matching folders (the Values).

Inside a Transformer layer, the input matrix X ∈ ℝ<sup>n × d</sup><sup>model</sup> (representing n tokens) is multiplied by three learned weight matrices—W<sup>Q</sup>, W<sup>K</sup>, and W<sup>V</sup>—to project every token simultaneously into its own Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) vectors:

blocks.raw: Q = XWQ,    K = XWK,    V = XWV

blocks.html: The attention mechanism then computes the compatibility of every query with every key via a dot product, scales the result, normalizes it into probabilities with a softmax function, and uses those probabilities to take a weighted sum of the values [4]:

blocks.raw:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QK^T
√(dk) )V

blocks.html: That denominator, √(dk) (where dk is the dimension of the query and key vectors), looks minor but is mathematically vital. If q and k have independent components with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product q · k has mean 0 and variance dk. When dk is large—say 64 or 128—raw dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into extreme saturation regions where its gradients approach zero [4]. Dividing by √(dk) restores unit variance and
keeps gradients healthy throughout training.

In autoregressive decoders (like GPT or Llama), the model must not peek at future tokens while predicting the next word. To enforce causality, a triangular causal mask adds -∞ to all entries above the main diagonal of QK^T before the softmax, forcing attention weights on future positions to exactly zero [4].

A single attention calculation produces only one set of weights per token, which forces the model to average together competing relationships. In a sentence like "The server dropped the connection because it ran out of memory," the pronoun "it" needs to link syntactically to "server" while also tracking the causal cue "because" and the semantic frame "ran out of memory."

Multi-head attention solves this by splitting the embedding space into h parallel subspaces— V [4]. In the Q, Wi K, Wi called attention heads—each with its own learned projection matrices Wi original Transformer base model, dmodel = 512 was divided across h = 8 heads of dimension dk = dv = 64, keeping the total computational cost roughly identical to single-head attention at full dimension [4]. The heads run in parallel, their outputs are concatenated, and a final linear projection WO mixes the results back into the model's residual stream:

blocks.html: In practice, different heads specialize spontaneously during training: some track local syntactic boundaries, others resolve pronouns across clauses, and others act as induction heads that copy previously seen patterns across long contexts.

blocks.text: Residual Connections, Normalization, and Feed-Forward Layers

blocks.html: Attention mixes information across tokens; the second half of every Transformer block—the position-wise feed-forward network (FFN)—processes each token's updated representation independently, adding nonlinear capacity and acting as a vast store of factual and linguistic associations.

Around both sublayers wrap residual (skip) connections, which add each sublayer's input directly to its output: x + Sublayer(x). Residual pathways give gradients an unobstructed superhighway back to the earliest layers during backpropagation, enabling networks to stack 80, 96, or more than 120 layers without collapsing.

Where normalization sits relative to those residual connections turned out to matter enormously. The 2017 Transformer placed Layer Normalization after the residual addition (Post-LN): LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) [4]. In February 2020, Ruibin Xiong and colleagues

proved theoretically and empirically that Post-LN produces disproportionately large gradients near the output layers at initialization, making training unstable without a delicate learning-rate warm-up schedule [10]. Moving normalization inside the residual branch before the sublayer
(Pre-LN)—x + Sublayer(LayerNorm(x))—kept gradients well-behaved across depth and became the universal standard for deep language models [10].
Two additional micro-architectural upgrades quietly replaced the 2017 defaults in almost every modern LLM:

1. RMSNorm: Standard LayerNorm normalizes activations by subtracting their mean (re-centering) and dividing by their standard deviation (re-scaling). In October 2019, Biao Zhang and Rico Sennrich hypothesized that re-centering was unnecessary and introduced Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (RMSNorm), which rescales solely by the root mean square of the activations [9]. Across diverse models, RMSNorm matched LayerNorm's accuracy while cutting normalization runtime by 7% to 64% [9].

2. SwiGLU Feed-Forward Blocks: Vaswani et al. used a two-layer MLP with a ReLU activation (max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2) [4]. In February 2020, Noam Shazeer tested Gated Linear Unit (GLU) variants inside Transformers and found that SwiGLU—which takes the element-wise product of two linear projections, one passed through the smooth Swish activation—consistently lowered pre-training perplexity and boosted downstream language understanding scores [11]:

blocks.raw: FFNSwiGLU(x) = (Swish1(xW) ⊗ xV)W2

blocks.html: With a minor hidden-dimension adjustment to keep parameter count constant, Pre-LN RMSNorm + RoPE + SwiGLU became the de facto "modern Transformer" template powering models from Llama 3 to DeepSeek-V3 [26] [27].

blocks.text: Five Lineages From One Blueprint: Architectural Families

blocks.html: The 2017 paper used both an encoder and a decoder because machine translation naturally maps a source sequence to a target sequence [4]. Within three years, researchers realized
that slicing the architecture apart—or feeding it non-text patches—unlocked entirely distinct families of AI systems.

blocks.text: Encoder-Only Models: BERT and Deep Bidirectional Understanding

blocks.html: In October 2018, Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova at Google AI released BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) [6]. BERT

discarded the decoder completely and kept only the encoder stack with unmasked bidirectional self-attention, allowing every token to attend to both left and right context simultaneously across all layers [6].

To pre-train a bidirectional model without letting tokens trivially "see themselves," Devlin et al. introduced Masked Language Modeling (MLM): randomly masking roughly 15% of input tokens and training the network to reconstruct them from surrounding context, paired with a Next Sentence Prediction objective [6]. Released in two flagship sizes—BERT-Base (12 layers, 110 million parameters) and BERT-Large (24 layers, 340 million parameters)—BERT shattered eleven natural language processing benchmarks at once, pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (a 7.7-point absolute jump) and SQuAD v1.1 question-answering F1 to 93.2 [6]. Encoder-only

Transformers remain workhorses for semantic search embeddings, document classification, reranking, and named-entity recognition, where understanding a whole passage cheaply matters more than generating fluent prose.

blocks.text: Decoder-Only Models: From GPT-1 to Llama 3

blocks.html: Four months before BERT, in June 2018, Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, and Ilya Sutskever at OpenAI took the opposite half of the 2017 architecture [5]. Their Generative

Pre-Trained Transformer (GPT) dropped the encoder and kept only the causally masked decoder, training it with the simplest possible objective: predict the next token given all preceding tokens [5]. That single 12-layer model improved state-of-the-art scores on 9 of 12 language benchmarks after task-specific fine-tuning [5].
The pivotal inflection point came in May 2020 with GPT-3 (Language Models are Few-Shot Learners) by Tom B. Brown and colleagues [8]. Scaled to 175 billion parameters, GPT-3

demonstrated that a pure autoregressive decoder did not even need gradient updates to tackle new tasks: showing the model a brief instruction and a handful of examples inside its prompt ("few-shot in-context learning") allowed it to translate, summarize, and write simple code on the fly [8].

Because every token in a training document provides a direct prediction target, decoder-only architectures proved extraordinarily sample-efficient and straightforward to scale. By July 2024, Meta's open-weight Llama 3 family demonstrated how far the dense decoder-only recipe could travel: its largest flagship model packed 405 billion parameters, supported a 128,000-token context window, and combined RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and grouped-query attention to rival top proprietary models across coding, multilingual reasoning, and tool use [26].

blocks.text: Encoder-Decoder Models: T5 and Unified Sequence-to-Sequence

blocks.html: While decoder-only models eventually captured the conversational AI spotlight, the full encoder-decoder architecture found a powerful synthesis in Colin Raffel and colleagues' October 2019 T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) [7]. T5 reframed every language task—

translation, summarization, sentiment analysis, even regression—into a single uniform interface: feed text in, generate text out. Trained on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4) with a span-corruption objective, T5 systematically mapped the design space of transfer learning and showed that full bidirectional encoding paired with autoregressive cross-attention decoding excelled at structured text-to-text transformations [7]. Encoder-decoder designs
also remain foundational in speech recognition and machine translation, where an acoustic or source-language encoder feeds a text decoder [30].

blocks.text: Vision Transformers (ViT): Breaking the Convolutional Monopoly

blocks.html: For nearly a decade after AlexNet (2012), computer vision belonged to convolutional neural networks (CNNs), whose sliding filters baked in spatial locality and translation equivariance. In October 2020, Alexey Dosovitskiy and colleagues at Google Research challenged that orthodoxy with An Image is Worth 16x16 Words [14].

The Vision Transformer (ViT) slices an input image into a flat grid of fixed-size patches— typically 16 × 16 pixels—flattens each patch into a vector via a linear projection, adds positional embeddings, and feeds the resulting sequence straight into a standard Transformer encoder [14]. On mid-sized datasets like ImageNet-1K alone, ViT initially trailed similarly sized ResNets

because it lacked CNNs' built-in spatial priors. Once pre-trained on massive image corpora, however, scale overwhelmed inductive bias: ViT matched or surpassed top convolutional networks on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and VTAB while requiring substantially less pre-training compute [14]. More importantly, turning images into sequences of patch tokens meant text and vision could share a single unified architecture, clearing the runway for native multimodal foundation models.

Generative image and video synthesis underwent a parallel transition. Early latent diffusion models relied on convolutional U-Net backbones to iteratively denoise visual latents. In December 2022, William Peebles (UC Berkeley) and Saining Xie (NYU) published Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers [15]. Their Diffusion Transformer (DiT) replaced the U-
Net entirely with a Transformer operating on latent patches, injecting timestep and class conditioning through adaptive layer normalization (adaLN-Zero) [15].

Peebles and Xie revealed a clean scaling law: increasing DiT's compute complexity (measured in Gflops) reliably drove down Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), achieving a state-of-the-art 2.27 FID on class-conditional 256 × 256 ImageNet generation at 118.6 Gflops [15]. That

predictable scaling directly inspired the next wave of image and video generators—most famously OpenAI's Sora (February 2024), which treats video as sequences of "spacetime patches" processed by a Diffusion Transformer backbone [31].

blocks.text: Scaling the Unscalable: Efficiency and Systems Engineering

blocks.html: If the 2017 Transformer had been left untouched, modern frontier AI would be economically impossible. Standard self-attention computes an n × n matrix for a sequence of length n: doubling the context length quadruples both compute and intermediate memory. Worse still, generating text one token at a time exposes an acute hardware mismatch. Over the past seven years, systems researchers have rebuilt almost every layer of Transformer execution to keep pace with GPU physics.

blocks.text: The KV Cache and the Memory-Bandwidth Wall

blocks.html: During inference, an autoregressive Transformer runs in two distinct regimes. In the prefill phase, the entire user prompt is processed in parallel, saturating GPU tensor cores (compute-bound). In the decode phase, the model generates one token per forward pass. Without optimization, generating token 1,001 would require recomputing the Key and Value projections for all 1,000 previous tokens.

To avoid redundant arithmetic, inference engines store past Key and Value tensors in GPU memory inside a KV cache. Each new token only computes its own qt, kt, vt, appends kt and vt to the cache, and attends over the stored history. Yet this creates a new bottleneck: at every single decoding step, the GPU must stream the entire KV cache—plus all model weights—from slow High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) into fast on-chip SRAM just to produce one token. Decoding becomes severely memory-bandwidth bound, leaving expensive compute units idle while waiting on memory transfers.

blocks.text: Shrinking the Cache: MQA, GQA, and Multi-head Latent Attention

blocks.html: In November 2019, Noam Shazeer diagnosed this exact memory-bandwidth bottleneck and proposed Multi-Query Attention (MQA) [16]. Instead of giving every attention head its own

Keys and Values, MQA shares a single Key head and a single Value head across all Query heads, slashing KV cache size and memory traffic by a factor equal to the number of heads— with only minor quality degradation [16].

In May 2023, Joshua Ainslie and colleagues at Google Research bridged the gap between standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and MQA with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [21]. GQA partitions Query heads into G groups, where each group shares one Key–Value head.

They also showed that existing MHA checkpoints could be "uptrained" into GQA using just 5% of original pre-training compute, achieving quality nearly indistinguishable from full MHA at decoding speeds close to MQA [21]. GQA rapidly became the industry default, adopted across Llama 3 and Mistral models [26] [24].
A further leap arrived in 2024 with Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), pioneered in DeepSeek-V2 and scaled in DeepSeek-V3 (December 2024) [27]. Rather than simply sharing

fewer full-size KV heads, MLA projects Keys and Values jointly down into a compact low-rank latent vector and caches only that compressed latent representation, reconstructing full multi-head Keys and Values on the fly through matrix absorption. This allows DeepSeek-V3 to dramatically compress KV cache memory without surrendering the representational richness of many distinct heads [27].

Even during training and prefill, standard attention wasted enormous time shuffling the massive n × n attention matrix back and forth between GPU HBM and on-chip SRAM. In May 2022, Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, and Christopher Ré introduced FlashAttention, an algorithm that computes mathematically exact attention—zero approximation—while never materializing the full n × n matrix in HBM [17].

FlashAttention slices Q, K, and V into small tiles that fit inside ultra-fast on-chip SRAM, fuses the dot product, masking, and an online softmax rescaling trick inside a single GPU kernel, and writes only the final output back to HBM [17]. In the backward pass, rather than storing
giant intermediate matrices, it recomputes attention tiles on the fly from saved normalization statistics—trading cheap extra arithmetic for massive HBM savings.
The FlashAttention lineage has since tracked each generation of GPU hardware:

FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao, July 2023) reordered loops, reduced non-matrix-multiply operations, and improved work partitioning across GPU warps, delivering roughly 2x faster backward passes than FlashAttention-1 and up to 10x speedups over standard PyTorch attention [18].

FlashAttention-3 (Jay Shah et al., July 2024) exploited asynchronous Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) hardware and FP8 low-precision tensor cores on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, overlapping data movement with matrix math [19].

FlashAttention-4 (Ted Zadouri et al., March 2026) co-designed kernel pipelining specifically for asymmetric hardware scaling on NVIDIA Blackwell B200 GPUs—where tensor-core math throughput has outpaced exponential/softmax units and shared memory bandwidth—reaching up to ~1,600 TFLOPS (71% of theoretical peak) in BF16 and running up to 1.3x faster than cuDNN and 2.7x faster than Triton baselines [20].

blocks.text: Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE): Decoupling Capacity From Compute

blocks.html: In a dense Transformer, every token activates 100% of the network's weights. Mixture of Experts (MoE) breaks that lockstep coupling by replacing each layer's single feed-forward block with a bank of parallel "expert" networks controlled by a lightweight learned router.
Noam Shazeer and colleagues demonstrated large-scale sparsely gated MoE layers in LSTM networks in January 2017 [22], and William Fedus, Barret Zoph, and Shazeer brought simplified

top-1 routing to Transformers with Switch Transformers in January 2021, scaling past a trillion parameters at constant per-token FLOPs [23]. The architecture hit mainstream open-source adoption in January 2024 with Mistral AI's Mixtral 8×7B [24]. At each layer, a router directs

every token to just 2 of 8 feed-forward experts; as a result, Mixtral commands 47 billion total parameters of stored knowledge while activating only 13 billion parameters per token during inference—matching or outperforming the dense Llama 2 70B model at a fraction of the inference cost [24].

By December 2024, DeepSeek-V3 pushed fine-grained MoE further still: 671 billion total parameters with just 37 billion activated per token, paired with an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing strategy and multi-token prediction [27]. Trained on 14.8 trillion tokens, the entire run required 2.788 million H800 GPU hours with zero irrecoverable loss spikes [27]—illustrating
how architectural sparsity and low-level systems engineering together bend the cost curve of frontier AI.

blocks.text: Ring Attention: Scaling Context Across Devices

blocks.html: Even with FlashAttention and GQA, a single GPU's memory eventually runs out when sequences stretch into millions of tokens—whole codebases, hours of video, or entire genomes. In October 2023, Hao Liu, Matei Zaharia, and Pieter Abbeel introduced Ring Attention [25]. Ring Attention shards a long sequence across multiple GPUs arranged in a

logical ring. While each device computes blockwise attention on its local Query chunk against its current Key–Value chunk, it asynchronously sends its Key–Value block to the next device in the ring and receives the next block in the background. Because communication overlaps with computation, memory scales linearly with the number of devices rather than hitting a single-chip wall—enabling exact attention over sequences exceeding 100 million tokens without approximation [25].

blocks.text: Beyond Language: Real-World Applications and Industry Case Studies

blocks.html: The deepest proof of the Transformer's generality is that its most celebrated breakthroughs now span domains that have nothing to do with English prose. Anywhere a problem can be framed as tokens interacting across space, time, or physical structure, attention has quietly taken over.

For fifty years, predicting a protein's three-dimensional atomic structure from its one-dimensional amino acid sequence stood as one of biology's grandest unsolved challenges. In July 2021, John Jumper and the Google DeepMind team published AlphaFold 2 in Nature, achieving atomic-level accuracy in the CASP14 assessment competitive with experimental X-ray crystallography [28]. At the heart of AlphaFold 2 sat the Evoformer, a specialized

Transformer variant that jointly applied attention across evolutionary multiple-sequence alignments and pairwise residue-distance matrices, enforcing geometric consistency through triangular attention updates.

In May 2024, AlphaFold 3 extended this paradigm beyond isolated proteins to jointly predict the 3D structures of proteins interacting with DNA, RNA, small-molecule drug ligands, ions, and post-translational modifications [29]. Replacing the Evoformer with a streamlined Pairformer paired with a diffusion module operating directly on atomic coordinates, AlphaFold 3 delivered markedly higher accuracy on protein–ligand docking and antibody–antigen interfaces than specialized physics-based tools [29].

blocks.text: Speech and Audio: Whisper's Scale-First Transcription

blocks.html: Automatic speech recognition once depended on brittle multi-stage pipelines combining acoustic models, pronunciation lexicons, and external language models. In December 2022, Alec Radford and colleagues at OpenAI introduced Whisper, an off-the-shelf encoder-decoder Transformer trained via large-scale weak supervision on multilingual audio-transcript pairs [30]. By converting audio into log-Mel spectrograms and letting a standard Transformer

encoder-decoder handle transcription, translation, and language identification end to end, Whisper achieved strong zero-shot robustness across accents, background noise, and technical jargon without dataset-specific fine-tuning [30].

blocks.text: Video Synthesis and Physical Simulation: Sora

blocks.html: In February 2024, OpenAI showcased Sora, a generalist video model capable of generating up to a full minute of high-definition video across varying resolutions and aspect ratios [31]. Architecturally, Sora built directly on Peebles and Xie's Diffusion Transformer [15]: a visual

encoder compresses raw video into a lower-dimensional latent grid, slices that grid into spacetime patches, and feeds them to a DiT that denoises entire scenes coherently across time [31]. Treating video frames as token sequences rather than fixed-size 3D grids allowed a
single model to handle portrait, widescreen, and square formats natively.

blocks.text: Open-Weight Enterprise Infrastructure: Llama 3 and Mixtral

blocks.html: In enterprise software, the combination of open-weight Transformer releases and inference optimizations has reshaped deployment economics. Organizations that cannot send proprietary source code, financial ledgers, or clinical records to third-party APIs now host open-weight models like Meta's Llama 3 (8B, 70B, and 405B) [26] or Mistral's Mixtral 8×7B [24] inside private cloud clusters. Pairing GQA and MoE sparsity with FlashAttention kernels

lets engineering teams serve 128,000-token contexts over internal documentation and codebases on modest multi-GPU footprints—turning what was a research curiosity in 2017 into routine corporate infrastructure.

blocks.text: Cracks in the Foundation: Limitations and Unresolved Questions

blocks.html: For all its dominance, the Transformer carries structural flaws that no amount of engineering polish has fully erased.

blocks.text: The Quadratic Tax and Growing Memory Footprints

blocks.html: FlashAttention cuts memory overhead from O(n<sup>2</sup>) to O(n), and Ring Attention distributes that

memory across clusters, yet the underlying arithmetic of dense self-attention remains stubbornly O(n2) in sequence length [4] [17]. At 1,000 tokens, quadratic attention is a rounding error compared to feed-forward matrix multiplications. At 1,000,000 tokens, attention dominates total compute. Meanwhile, the KV cache still grows linearly with every token added to a conversation or agentic workflow. Serving thousands of concurrent users with 100K-token sessions remains a brutal memory-capacity and memory-bandwidth problem, especially as AI systems shift toward long "test-time compute" reasoning chains that generate tens of thousands of intermediate tokens per query [38].

A subtler limitation lives in computational complexity theory. Because a standard Transformer has a fixed number of layers and processes tokens in parallel, its expressive power has hard mathematical boundaries. In 2020, Michael Hahn proved that self-attention—both soft and hard—cannot reliably model certain formal languages, including periodic finite-state machines (such as checking parity over arbitrarily long bit strings) or deeply nested hierarchical structures, unless the number of layers or heads grows with input length [32].

In 2022–2023, William Merrill and Ashish Sabharwal sharpened this result, showing that log-precision Transformers reside inside the uniform constant-depth threshold circuit class TC0 [33]. Practically, this means a single forward pass of a Transformer struggles with exact

sequential state tracking—problems like composing long chains of permutations, verifying intricate chess move sequences, or mentally executing multi-step code without writing intermediate steps down. Chain-of-thought prompting partially bypasses this ceiling by externalizing intermediate state into generated tokens, effectively turning the context window into scratchpad memory—at the steep cost of extra latency and token generation.

blocks.text: Data Exhaustion, Interpretability, and Energy Concentration

blocks.html: Beyond mathematics, Transformers are famously data-hungry. Because self-attention imposes minimal structural priors on how inputs relate, frontier models routinely consume tens of trillions of training tokens—14.8 trillion for DeepSeek-V3 [27] and 15 trillion for Llama 3 [26]—

exhausting high-quality public web text and forcing labs toward synthetic data and reinforcement learning. Simultaneously, mechanistic interpretability remains an open frontier: while researchers can identify individual attention heads or sparse features, explaining why a 400-billion-parameter network hallucinates a plausible-sounding citation or fails a simple logical inversion remains far from solved.

blocks.text: Current Developments: State Space Models and the Hybrid Turn

blocks.html: The quadratic wall has fueled a serious search for sub-quadratic successors—architectures that keep the Transformer's parallel training speed while restoring an RNN's constant-memory, linear-time inference.

The most credible challenger emerged from State Space Models (SSMs), rooted in classical control theory. Early deep SSMs could train in parallel via convolutions, but their time-invariant dynamics struggled on discrete language tasks because they could not selectively remember or ignore specific tokens.
In December 2023, Albert Gu and Tri Dao introduced Mamba, making the SSM's state-transition parameters functions of the current input token [35]. That input-dependent

selectivity let the model dynamically filter noise and retain key facts, while a custom hardware-aware parallel scan kept training fast on GPUs. Mamba achieved O(n) linear scaling in sequence length, constant O(1) inference state memory, and up to 5x higher inference throughput than comparable Transformers, with Mamba-3B matching Transformers twice its size on language modeling benchmarks [35].
In May 2024, Dao and Gu bridged the two worlds with Mamba-2 (Transformers are SSMs), formulating Structured State Space Duality (SSD) [36]. SSD proved mathematically that

structured SSMs and certain forms of linear attention are dual decompositions of the same class of semiseparable matrices, enabling Mamba-2 to rely on hardware-friendly matrix multiplications and run 2x to 8x faster than Mamba-1 [36].

Yet pure SSMs hit two stubborn walls. First, compressing an entire history into a fixed-size recurrent state degrades exact verbatim recall over long contexts ("needle-in-a-haystack" retrieval). Second, in April 2024, William Merrill, Jackson Petty, and Ashish Sabharwal published The Illusion of State in State-Space Models, proving that standard real-valued diagonal SSMs—like Mamba—also fall within the same TC0 complexity class as Transformers and struggle on the very same state-tracking tasks [34].
In March 2026, Aakash Lahoti, Tri Dao, Albert Gu, and collaborators directly targeted those weaknesses with Mamba-3 [38]. Designed from an inference-first perspective for agentic and

test-time compute workloads, Mamba-3 introduced exponential-trapezoidal discretization, complex-valued state updates specifically to improve state tracking, and a multi-input, multi-output (MIMO) formulation that boosted modeling power without increasing decode latency [38]. At the 1.5B parameter scale, Mamba-3's MIMO variant improved average downstream accuracy by 1.8 percentage points over Gated DeltaNet while matching Mamba-2's perplexity at half the state size [38].

Rather than betting everything on pure attention or pure recurrence, production engineering has increasingly converged on hybrid architectures. In March 2024, Opher Lieber and colleagues at AI21 Labs introduced Jamba, interleaving Transformer attention layers with Mamba SSM layers and sparse MoE blocks [37]. The 52-billion-parameter model (12 billion

active parameters per token) slashed KV cache memory drastically—because only a small fraction of layers needed attention caches—allowing long-context inference to fit on a single 80GB GPU while retaining strong exact retrieval [37].

By 2025 and 2026, hybrid token mixing—combining fast recurrent layers (such as Mamba-2/3 or Gated DeltaNet), exact local sliding-window attention, and periodic global attention layers— has become one of the most active design patterns in open-weight modeling, pairing constant-memory context compression with exact long-distance lookup where it counts.

blocks.text: Future Outlook: What Comes After Pure Attention?

blocks.html: Note: Whereas the preceding sections document verified research and deployed systems through 2026, the following outlook represents informed forward-looking analysis of emerging trajectories rather than settled fact.

The era of the vanilla, dense, all-global-attention Transformer as the default blueprint for every frontier model appears to be nearing its twilight—not because attention failed, but because specialization is winning. Over the next three to five years, several architectural shifts look increasingly likely.

First, hybrid attention–recurrence backbones will probably become the standard workhorse for long-context and agentic AI. Pure attention pays too steep a memory-bandwidth tax when models generate 50,000-token reasoning traces or ingest multi-hour video streams; pure state-space models still lose precision on exact multi-document lookup. Interleaving linear-time recurrent layers with sparse global attention layers—combined with fine-grained Mixture of Experts—offers a practical sweet spot that preserves exact recall without blowing out GPU memory budgets.

Second, algorithm–hardware co-design will dictate architectural winners as much as pure mathematical elegance. As FlashAttention-4's Blackwell optimizations [20] and Mamba-3's inference-first MIMO design [38] illustrate, the gap between theoretical FLOPs and real-world

wall-clock speed on modern accelerators is widening. Future architectures will likely be designed from day one around low-precision arithmetic (FP8 and FP4), asynchronous memory hierarchies, and disaggregated serving clusters that separate compute-heavy prefill nodes from bandwidth-hungry decode nodes.

Third, adaptive, test-time compute could reshape how networks allocate depth and attention dynamically. Instead of routing every trivial punctuation mark through the same 100 layers of global attention as a knotty mathematical proof, emerging research points toward architectures that dynamically vary expert count, recurrence depth, and attention span token by token. Whether the resulting systems are still called "Transformers" or earn a new umbrella name, self-attention itself is unlikely to disappear; it is far more likely to settle into its permanent role as the high-precision random-access memory inside broader, heterogeneous neural computers.

Looking back nearly a decade after Attention Is All You Need [4], the Transformer's deepest lesson is deceptively understated. It did not triumph because it mimicked the human brain or encoded clever linguistic rules. It triumphed because it stripped away sequential constraints, gave every element in a sequence a direct mathematical line of sight to every other element, and expressed the entire calculation in the native language of modern parallel hardware.

From BERT's bidirectional encoders and GPT's autoregressive decoders to ViT's image patches, DiT's latent video worlds, and AlphaFold's molecular geometry, that single architectural core proved adaptable enough to unify fields that had spent decades growing apart. Today, as FlashAttention kernels, latent KV compression, sparse Mixtures of Experts, and Mamba-style state spaces reshape the architecture from the inside out, the Transformer is no longer a static 2017 diagram—it is a living engineering platform, still defining the frontier of intelligent computing.

1. Why did Transformers replace RNNs and LSTMs for language modeling? Recurrent networks like RNNs and LSTMs process text one token at a time, meaning step t cannot be computed until step t-1 finishes. This sequential dependency prevents parallelization across a sentence during training and forces distant words to communicate across long chains of hidden states. Transformers replace recurrence with self-attention, giving every token a direct O(1) connection to every other token and allowing entire training sequences to be processed simultaneously on GPUs [4].

2. What do Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) vectors actually represent? They are three distinct linear projections of each token's embedding learned during training. Conceptually, a token's Query represents what information it is looking for, its Key advertises what information it contains, and its Value holds the actual payload passed forward. Comparing a Query against all Keys via dot products produces attention weights that determine how much of each token's Value gets blended into the output [4].

3. Why does scaled dot-product attention divide by √(dk)? When the key vector dimension dk is large, raw dot products between queries and keys grow large in variance. Feeding large numbers into the softmax function pushes it into flat saturation zones where gradients shrink toward zero, stalling learning. Dividing by √(dk) normalizes the variance back to roughly 1, keeping gradients stable during backpropagation [4].

4. What is the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder Transformers? Encoder-only models (such as BERT) use bidirectional attention so every token sees both left and right context, making them ideal for embeddings, search, and classification [6]. Decoder-only models (such as GPT and Llama) apply a causal mask so tokens only attend to earlier tokens, optimizing them for autoregressive text generation [5] [26]. Encoder-decoder
models (such as T5 and Whisper) pair both halves via cross-attention, excelling at mapping one sequence modality or language into another [7] [30].

5. Why do modern LLMs use RoPE instead of the original 2017 sinusoidal positional encodings? Original sinusoidal encodings add fixed absolute position signals to token embeddings at the input layer, which degrades when models encounter sequences longer than their training window. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) instead rotates Query and Key vectors by position-dependent angles inside attention, naturally encoding relative token distances with smooth long-range decay and stronger length flexibility [12].

6. Does FlashAttention approximate self-attention to make it faster? No. FlashAttention computes mathematically exact self-attention. Its speed and memory gains come from IO-awareness: it tiles the Query, Key, and Value matrices into fast on-chip GPU SRAM and uses an online softmax trick so the massive n × n attention matrix never has to be written to or read from slower High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) [17].

7. How does a Mixture of Experts (MoE) Transformer reduce inference costs? An MoE Transformer replaces each layer's single dense feed-forward network with multiple parallel expert networks and a learned router. For each token, the router activates only a small subset of experts (for example, 2 of 8 in Mixtral 8×7B, activating 13B of 47B total parameters [24], or 37B of 671B in DeepSeek-V3 [27]). This lets a model store vast knowledge while spending far fewer FLOPs per generated token.

8. Will State Space Models like Mamba completely replace Transformers? Not in the foreseeable future. Mamba and its successors (Mamba-2 and Mamba-3) offer linear O(n) scaling and constant-memory inference [35] [38], but compressing history into a fixed recurrent state still trails full attention on exact long-range retrieval. Current industry momentum favors hybrid architectures like Jamba that interleave fast SSM layers with periodic Transformer attention layers to get the best of both worlds [37].

title: How AI Models Evaluate and Generate Predictions
deck: Every prediction an AI system makes—whether flagging a hospital patient for sepsis, approving a loan, or selecting the next word in a sentence—is the product of raw mathematical scores, deliberate decoding rules, and rigorous evaluation. This guide unpacks how modern models turn inputs into outputs and how engineers measure whether those predictions can be trusted.

Every prediction an AI system makes—whether flagging a hospital patient for sepsis, approving a loan, or selecting the next word in a sentence—is the product of raw mathematical scores, deliberate decoding rules, and rigorous evaluation. This guide unpacks how modern models turn inputs into outputs and how engineers measure whether those predictions can be trusted.

blocks.text: The Moment of Truth: Why Inference Matters as Much as Training

blocks.html: Training an artificial intelligence model captures most of the public imagination. Headlines track billions of parameters, vast GPU clusters, and months-long optimization runs that adjust weights through gradient descent and backpropagation (see How Machine Learning Models Are Trained and Gradient Descent and Backpropagation Explained). Yet once training ends and a model's weights are frozen, the system has still done nothing useful. Its real value—and its real capacity to cause harm—emerges only during inference, the moment the model encounters unfamiliar data and must produce a prediction.

Consider two seemingly unrelated events happening in the same second. In a hospital ward, an electronic health record system ingests a patient's latest vital signs and lab values, runs them through a risk model, and decides whether to trigger an urgent sepsis alert for the nursing staff. Half a world away, a software engineer types a bug report into a coding assistant, and a large language model begins streaming a multi-file patch one token at a time. On the surface, these systems look entirely different. Underneath, both are executing the same fundamental cycle: transforming raw inputs into numerical representations, passing them through learned mathematical transformations to produce unnormalized scores, converting those scores into probability distributions, and applying a decision or decoding rule to emit a final prediction.

Just as critical is the mirror image of generation: evaluation. A prediction is only as trustworthy as the yardstick used to test it. A model that scores 95% accuracy on a benchmark can fail catastrophically in a clinic if 93% of patients are healthy. A language model that generates eloquent prose can fabricate legal citations with serene confidence. A self-driving perception stack that detects cars cleanly in sunny Arizona can stumble in Boston rain. Understanding modern AI requires looking at prediction generation and prediction evaluation not as separate phases, but as two interlocking halves of one engineering discipline.

blocks.text: From Weather Forecasts to Neural Logits: A Brief History

blocks.html: The problem of judging probabilistic predictions is far older than deep learning. In January 1950, Glenn W. Brier, a statistician at the United States Weather Bureau, published a three-page paper in Monthly Weather Review proposing a mathematical rule for verifying weather forecasts expressed as probabilities [1]. Brier recognized a trap that still plagues AI teams

seventy-six years later: if you only grade forecasters on binary right-or-wrong calls, you cannot tell the difference between a forecaster who honestly reports a 60% chance of rain and one who overconfidently declares a 99% chance. His Brier score—the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual binary outcomes—rewarded both accuracy and honesty, scoring a perfect forecaster at 0 and a constant 50% hedger at 0.25 [1].

For decades, statistical machine learning stayed close to those roots. Logistic regression, decision trees, and early shallow neural networks such as Yann LeCun's five-layer LeNet-5 in 1998 produced outputs that behaved reasonably well as probabilities [2]. Evaluation remained

tightly scoped to narrow tasks. When machine translation researchers needed a faster alternative to human translators in 2002, Kishore Papineni and colleagues at IBM introduced BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy), which measured exact word-sequence overlap against human reference translations [3]. Two years later, Chin-Yew Lin at the University of Southern California introduced ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) to score automated document summaries in NIST's Document Understanding Conference [4].

Two architectural shifts upended that tidy landscape. First, the deep learning wave of the 2010s introduced networks with dozens or hundreds of layers—such as 110-layer Residual Networks (ResNets)—that slashed classification error rates while quietly breaking probability calibration [2]. Second, the rise of Transformer-based foundation models (see What Are

Foundation Models? and Understanding Transformers: The Architecture Behind Modern AI) replaced single-label classification with open-ended, autoregressive generation. Instead of choosing one label from ten categories, a model now chooses one token from a vocabulary of 50,000 to 200,000 possibilities, hundreds or thousands of times in a row. Generating a good prediction suddenly required sophisticated sampling algorithms, and evaluating it required rethinking what "correctness" even means when a thousand different answers can be right.

blocks.text: Inside the Inference Pipeline: From Raw Input to Probability Distributions

blocks.html: Whether a system predicts house prices, classifies X-rays, or writes Python code, inference follows a deterministic computational pipeline right up until the final selection step.

blocks.text: Input Representation and the Forward Pass

blocks.html: Machine learning models cannot read text, see pixels, or interpret medical charts directly. Every input must first be encoded into tensors—multidimensional arrays of floating-point numbers. Tabular models normalize numeric features and encode categorical variables into dense vectors. Computer vision models convert pixel grids into normalized color channels or patch embeddings. Large language models split raw text into subword units called tokens, mapping each token ID to a high-dimensional vector known as an embedding.

Once encoded, the input enters the forward pass. Data flows sequentially through the model's layers—linear matrix multiplications, convolutional filters, or Transformer self-attention blocks —interspersed with nonlinear activation functions and normalization layers. Each layer extracts progressively more abstract structure: edges become object parts in a vision network; syntax and local phrasing become semantic intent and logical constraints in a language model.

In autoregressive Transformers, the forward pass splits into two computationally distinct phases. During the prefill phase, the model processes the entire input prompt in parallel, computing key and value matrices for every token and storing them in GPU memory as the KV cache. This phase is compute-bound: the GPU's arithmetic units run near peak utilization. During the decode phase, the model generates one new token per forward pass, reading the accumulated KV cache from memory at every step. This phase is memory-bandwidth-bound, which is why generating a 500-token answer takes dramatically longer than reading a 500-token prompt.

At the final layer of a classification or language model sits a linear projection head. It multiplies the final hidden state by an output weight matrix to produce a vector of raw, unnormalized real numbers called logits, denoted z = (z1, z2, …, zV), where V is the number of classes or the
vocabulary size. Logits can be positive, negative, or arbitrarily large; they represent relative preferences, not probabilities.

To convert logits into a valid probability distribution whose entries lie between 0 and 1 and sum to 1, models apply the softmax function. In modern inference systems, softmax is almost always paired with a positive scalar parameter T called temperature:

blocks.raw:
P(y = i | x) = 
exp(zi / T)
∑j=1
V exp(zj / T)

blocks.html: Here, z<sub>i</sub> is the raw logit for candidate class or token i, and T > 0 reshapes the distribution's entropy before exponentiation. When T = 1, softmax uses the raw logits unchanged. As T → 0, dividing by a tiny number magnifies the gap between the highest logit and every runner-up, concentrating nearly all probability mass on the single top candidate. When T > 1, the differences between logits shrink, flattening the distribution and giving lower-ranked candidates a higher chance of being selected.

A common misconception is that softmax outputs represent true statistical probabilities of correctness. Mathematically, softmax only guarantees that the numbers are non-negative and sum to one; it offers no guarantee that an event assigned a 0.90 score will actually occur 90% of the time in reality [2]. How a system turns that distribution into a concrete prediction
depends on whether the task is discriminative or generative.

blocks.text: Discriminative Prediction: Thresholds, Trade-Offs, and Scoring Rules

blocks.html: Discriminative models map an input x directly to a target label or continuous number y. Spam filters, fraud detectors, medical triage models, and demand forecasters all fall into this family. Because their outputs are compact and structured, evaluation focuses on quantifying errors against ground-truth labels—a suite of methods standardized in libraries such as scikit-learn [5].

blocks.text: Classification Thresholds and the Illusion of Accuracy

blocks.html: A binary classifier outputs a single score p̂ ∈ [0, 1] estimating the likelihood of the positive class. Turning p̂ into a hard decision ("flag transaction as fraud" vs. "approve") requires choosing a decision threshold τ. By default, software packages set τ = 0.5, but in real-world deployments 0.5 is rarely optimal. Raising τ reduces false alarms at the cost of missing genuine cases; lowering τ catches more genuine cases at the cost of flooding human reviewers with false positives.
Every threshold choice induces a confusion matrix tallying four outcomes: True Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), True Negatives (TN), and False Negatives (FN) [5]. From those four counts

flow the workhorse metrics of classification. Accuracy—(TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)—is intuitive but treacherous whenever classes are imbalanced. If only 1% of credit card transactions are fraudulent, a trivial model that predicts "legitimate" every time achieves 99% accuracy while catching zero fraud.

To expose that failure, practitioners evaluate Precision (the fraction of positive alerts that are genuinely positive, TP / (TP + FP)) alongside Recall (the fraction of all genuine positives the model caught, TP / (TP + FN)) [5]. Because precision and recall pull against each other as the threshold moves, engineers frequently summarize their balance with the F1 score, their harmonic mean:

blocks.raw:
F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall
Precision + Recall

2TP
2TP + FP + FN

blocks.html: Unlike an arithmetic average, the harmonic mean punishes extreme lopsidedness: a model with 1.00 recall and 0.02 precision earns an arithmetic average of 0.51, but an F1 score of just 0.039.

To evaluate a classifier's ranking quality across all possible thresholds at once, engineers plot the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, which traces True Positive Rate (Recall) against False Positive Rate (FP / (FP + TN)), and compute the Area Under the ROC Curve (ROC-AUC) [5]. An ROC-AUC of 0.5 corresponds to random guessing, while 1.0 indicates perfect separation. Yet even ROC-AUC can flatter a model on heavily skewed datasets, because a large pool of true negatives keeps the false positive rate deceptively small even when false alarms vastly outnumber true alerts. In rare-event domains like sepsis detection or fraud, the Precision-Recall (PR) curve and its area (Average Precision) provide a far sharper picture of operational pain.

When a model predicts a continuous value—such as energy load in megawatts, delivery time in minutes, or property value—classification thresholds do not apply. Evaluation instead measures the distance between predictions ŷ i and true targets yi across n examples [5]. Mean

Absolute Error (MAE) averages |y<sub>i</sub> - ŷ i|, treating every unit of error linearly and resisting distortion from occasional outliers. Mean Squared Error (MSE) averages (y<sub>i</sub> - ŷ i)<sup>2</sup> (and its

square root, RMSE, restores the original units), heavily penalizing large misses—crucial when a single massive error is far worse than ten small ones. Finally, the coefficient of determination (R2) compares the model's squared error against a naive baseline that simply predicts the dataset mean, indicating what proportion of variance the model explains [5].

blocks.text: Generative Decoding: Turning Probabilities Into Sequences

blocks.html: Discriminative models emit a single answer and stop. Autoregressive generative models—most prominently large language models—factorize the probability of an entire sequence y = (y<sub>1</sub>, y<sub>2</sub>, …, y<sub>T</sub>) into a chain of conditional next-token predictions:

blocks.raw:
P(y1, …, yT | x) = ∏t=1
T P(yt | y, x)

blocks.html: At each step t, the model produces a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary, chooses one token y<sub>t</sub>, appends it to the context, and runs another forward pass. The algorithm
governing that choice is called a decoding strategy, and as researchers discovered in the late 2010s, decoding choices can make the exact same neural network sound either incisive or broken [6].

blocks.text: The Paradox of Likelihood: Greedy Decoding and Beam Search

blocks.html: The most straightforward decoding rule is greedy decoding: at every step, pick the single token with the highest probability (argmaxi P(yt = i | y, x)). Greedy decoding is fast and

deterministic, making it useful for strict factual extraction or deterministic code completion, yet it suffers from myopia. Choosing the locally best word at step 3 can trap the sentence in an awkward grammatical cul-de-sac by step 12.

Beam search attempts to fix that myopia by tracking the top B most probable partial sequences (beams) in parallel at every step, expanding each beam and retaining the B highest-scoring cumulative sequences. Beam search became the gold standard for machine translation and speech recognition, where the output space is tightly constrained by the source input.

Yet when researchers applied greedy decoding and beam search to open-ended text generation, something bizarre happened. In a landmark April 2019 paper presented at ICLR 2020, "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration," Ari Holtzman, Jan Buys, Li Du, Maxwell Forbes, and Yejin Choi demonstrated that maximizing sequence likelihood produces text that is bland, generic, and prone to endless repetition loops [6]. Human writing, they showed, does

not hover at the peak of predictability; it exhibits a lively, fluctuating rhythm of surprising word choices interspersed with predictable glue words. A high-probability loop ("I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.") actually accumulates higher per-token likelihood under a neural language model than a vivid, coherent human paragraph [6].

blocks.text: Stochastic Truncation: Top-k, Nucleus (Top-p), and Min-p Sampling

blocks.html: Pure random sampling from the full softmax distribution breaks repetition loops, but introduces the opposite failure: the "unreliable tail." Across a 100,000-token vocabulary, tens of thousands of nonsensical tokens each receive tiny nonzero probabilities (say, 10-5). Summed together, those garbage tokens can capture 10% to 20% of the total probability mass, guaranteeing that sooner or later the sampler will draw an absurd word that derails the entire paragraph [6].
To preserve diversity while pruning the tail, engineers rely on truncation samplers combined with temperature scaling:

Top-k Sampling: Popularized by Angela Fan, Mike Lewis, and Yann Dauphin in their July 2018 ACL paper "Hierarchical Neural Story Generation," top-k restricts sampling to the k most probable tokens (for example, k = 10 or k = 40) and renormalizes their probabilities [7]. Its flaw is

rigidity. When the model is nearly certain of the next word ("The capital of France is ___"), a fixed k = 40 still admits 39 wrong words. Conversely, when the context is genuinely open-ended ("She opened the box and found a ___"), a fixed k = 10 cuts off dozens of sensible choices [6].

Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling: Introduced by Holtzman et al. (2019), nucleus sampling solves that rigidity dynamically [6]. Instead of fixing the count of allowed tokens, it fixes the cumulative probability mass p (commonly p = 0.90 or 0.95) and samples from the smallest top-ranked set of tokens whose probabilities sum to at least p. When the model is confident, the nucleus automatically shrinks to one or two tokens; when the distribution is flat, the nucleus expands to dozens or hundreds [6].

Min-p Sampling: Proposed in July 2024 by Nguyen Nhat Minh, Andrew Baker, Clement Neo, Allen Roush, and Andreas Kirsch in "Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs," min-p sets a dynamic floor relative to the top token's probability: any token with probability below pbase × pmax is discarded [8]. The method gained rapid adoption in

open-source inference engines for keeping high-temperature outputs coherent. Still, scientific scrutiny continues: a June 2025 independent re-analysis ("A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models") audited the original benchmarks, human evaluations, and sweeps, concluding that relative to well-tuned standard samplers, min-p does not consistently improve the quality-diversity trade-off [9]. The debate underscores an important engineering lesson: decoding hyperparameters interact heavily with model scale and post-training alignment, and no single truncation rule dominates every workload.

blocks.text: Speculative Decoding: Accelerating Generation Without Changing the Math

blocks.html: Because autoregressive decoding generates one token per serial forward pass, serving a 70-billion-parameter or frontier model is painfully slow and underutilizes GPU compute. In November 2022 (published at ICML 2023), Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias at Google Research introduced speculative decoding to break this serial bottleneck [10].

The insight is deceptively simple: many tokens in a sentence—articles, punctuation, boilerplate syntax—are easy to predict and do not require a giant model. Speculative decoding pairs the large target model with a tiny, fast draft model. The draft model rapidly proposes K candidate tokens in sequence. The large target model then evaluates all K candidate tokens simultaneously in a single parallel forward pass, verifying each token against its own probability distribution [10]. Using a modified rejection-sampling scheme, the algorithm

accepts all valid prefix tokens and, at the first rejected position, resamples from the adjusted residual distribution. Mathematically, the resulting output distribution is provably identical to sampling directly from the large model alone—zero quality loss—yet Leviathan et al. demonstrated a 2× to 3× wall-clock speedup on T5-XXL without retraining or modifying model weights [10].
